Streamlining Contested Adjudications in Licensing Proceedings

AGENCY: Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

ACTION: Final rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC, agency, or 
Commission) is revising the agency's rules of practice and procedure to 
streamline contested adjudications in NRC licensing proceedings in 
response to the Accelerating Deployment of Versatile, Advanced Nuclear 
for Clean Energy Act of 2024 (ADVANCE Act) and Executive Order 14300, 
Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

DATES: This final rule is effective on December 3, 2026, and applies to 
contested adjudicatory proceedings noticed on or after the effective 
date.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

Executive Summary

A. Need for the Regulatory Action

    The Accelerating Deployment of Versatile, Advanced Nuclear for 
Clean Energy Act of 2024 (ADVANCE Act) was signed into law in July of 
2024. The ADVANCE Act establishes requirements to enhance the NRC's 
timeliness and efficiency, including a broad requirement for efficiency 
through an updated Mission Statement.\1\ As directly relevant to the 
hearing process, ADVANCE Act Sec.  505(b) requires the NRC to provide 
``efficient and timely . . . proceedings'' for a broad category of 
licensing actions, and ADVANCE Act Sec.  207(c) requires the NRC (for 
certain reactor combined license applications) to, among other things, 
complete ``any necessary public licensing hearings and related 
processes'' not later than two years after docketing the application, 
to the maximum extent practicable.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ ADVANCE Act of 2024, Public Law 118-67, div. B, Sec. Sec.  
206, 207, 501, 504, 505, 506 (2024). For example, Section 506 
requires the NRC to periodically improve its performance metrics and 
milestone schedules for completing safety evaluations ``to provide 
the most efficient metrics and schedules reasonably achievable.''
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Subsequently, the President directed a series of reforms to improve 
the agency's efficiency and effectiveness in the May 23, 2025, 
Executive Order (E.O.) 14300, ``Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear 
Regulatory Commission'' (90 FR 22587, May 29, 2025). As relevant to 
this final rule, section 5(j) of E.O. 14300 directs the NRC to 
streamline its public hearing process. Relatedly, E.O. 14300 section 
5(a) directs the NRC to establish fixed deadlines for its evaluation 
and approval of specified licensing actions and requests, section 5(d) 
directs the NRC to establish an expedited approval pathway for reactor 
designs tested and demonstrated by the Department of Defense (also 
referred to as the Department of War (DOW)) \2\ or the Department of 
Energy (DOE), and section 5(e) directs the NRC to ``[e]stablish a 
process for high-volume licensing of microreactors and modular 
reactors[.]''
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \2\ The Department of Defense (DOD) was authorized to use the 
secondary title, the Department of War (DOW), in September 2025 by 
Executive Order. See Executive Order No. 14347, ``Restoring the 
United States Department of War,'' 90 FR 43893 (dated September 5, 
2025; published September 10, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In response to Congressional and Executive action, the NRC has 
developed this final rule focused on streamlining the agency's rules of 
practice and procedure. The changes to the contested hearing process 
will reduce burden, increase clarity, and promote efficiencies in line 
with deadlines established in accordance with the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 
14300.

B. Major Provisions

    Major provisions of this final rule include the following:

 Revisions to the contested hearing process that will 
enable the NRC to generally complete adjudications within 11 to 13.5 
months or faster for expedited proceedings.

 A requirement for evidentiary hearings to begin as soon as 
practicable upon admission of contentions.

 Strict deadlines for the completion of hearings.

 Tailored hearing schedules that correspond to the staff's 
review schedule to the maximum extent practicable, considering the 
complexity of the application.

 A reduction in discovery burden on all parties to focus on 
information of highest value and reflect the greater availability of 
information due to technological developments.

 Revisions to accelerate Commission review of appeals.

 Elimination, refinement, or addition of provisions that 
will accommodate the schedule directives of the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 
14300.

C. Costs and Benefits

    This final rule is considered to be a deregulatory action and will 
reduce burden for both the government and hearing participants by 
streamlining contested hearing proceedings. Over the five-year analysis 
period (2026-2030), the revisions to the contested hearing procedures 
are projected to yield savings for the public, the industry, and 
government. The combined net savings would generate cumulative 
undiscounted savings of $67.4 million. Using 2025 as the base year, the 
net present value (NPV) of these net savings is $61.7 million, 
discounted at 3 percent, or $55.2 million, discounted at 7 percent. The 
projected annualized cost savings would be $13.5 million

[[Page 69447]]

discounted at 3 percent, or $13.5 million discounted at 7 percent. 
These values represent net savings, as implementation and transition 
costs are expected to be minimal.
    For more information, please see the regulatory analysis included 
later in this notice.

I. Executive Order 14300: Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory 
Commission

    On May 23, 2025, the President signed E.O. 14300, ``Ordering the 
Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.'' Section 5, ``Reforming 
and Modernizing the NRC's Regulations,'' directs the NRC to undertake a 
review and wholesale revision of its regulations and guidance documents 
as guided by the policies set forth in section 2 of the E.O. This 
rulemaking addresses section 5(j), which directs the NRC to 
``[s]treamline the public hearings process,'' and also supports meeting 
the objectives of sections 5(a), 5(d), and 5(e) of E.O. 14300, as 
discussed below.

II. Background

    Since its inception, the Commission has periodically taken steps to 
assess and improve the efficiency of its adjudicatory process, as 
discussed in a 2004 rule (69 FR 2182, pages 2182 through 2186, January 
14, 2004) (hereafter ``2004 Adjudications Rule''). Generally, these 
reforms have yielded less formal adjudications intended to reduce the 
burden of litigation costs for all parties and remove procedural 
mechanisms that are not essential to developing an adequate hearing 
record. The Commission last finalized a major reformation of its 
hearing processes in 2004 in anticipation of a significant volume of 
new proceedings to consider applications for new facilities, to renew 
operating licenses, to reflect restructuring in the electric utility 
industry, and to license waste storage facilities.
    The Commission now expects a similar increase in licensing 
applications in the coming years, and Congress and the President have 
directed the NRC to prepare to review and process these applications as 
expeditiously as possible. In 2024, Congress passed the ADVANCE Act, 
which established requirements to enhance the NRC's timeliness and 
efficiency, such as the direction to update the NRC's mission statement 
to provide that the NRC's licensing and regulation of the civilian use 
of radioactive materials and nuclear energy be conducted in a manner 
that is efficient and does not unnecessarily limit--(1) the civilian 
use of radioactive materials and deployment of nuclear energy; or (2) 
the benefits of civilian use of radioactive materials and nuclear 
energy technology to society. The ADVANCE Act also addresses the 
hearing process, with section 505(b) amending the Atomic Energy Act of 
1954, as amended (AEA) section 181 to require the NRC to provide 
``efficient and timely . . . proceedings'' for a broad category of 
licensing actions. Also, for certain reactor combined license 
applications, section 207(c) of the ADVANCE Act requires the NRC, to 
the maximum extent practicable, to (1) complete safety and 
environmental reviews not later than 18 months of docketing, (2) 
complete ``any necessary public licensing hearings and related 
processes'' not later than two years after docketing, and (3) make a 
final decision on whether to issue the combined license not later than 
25 months after docketing.\3\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \3\ This expedited process applies only to applicants for 
combined licenses who meet certain requirements regarding, among 
other things, the use of previously approved designs on existing 
commercial reactor sites (or on substantially similar sites adjacent 
thereto), as described in Sec.  207(b).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Building on the ADVANCE Act, the President signed E.O. 14300 
``Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission,'' on May 
23, 2025 (90 FR 22587, May 29, 2025). Section 3 of E.O. 14300 directs 
the NRC to consider the benefits of increased availability of, and 
innovation in, nuclear power to the nation's economic and national 
security in addition to safety, health, and environmental 
considerations, when the NRC carries out its licensing and related 
regulatory functions. In furtherance of the President's directive, E.O. 
14300 tasked the NRC with streamlining its public hearing process. As 
relevant here, section 5 of E.O. 14300 directs the NRC to undertake a 
review and wholesale revision of its regulations and guidance documents 
and establishes specific tasks this effort must encompass, including 
streamlining the public hearings process, as directed by section 5(j).
    Relatedly, section 5(a) of the E.O. directs the NRC to establish 
fixed deadlines for its evaluation and approval of specified licensing 
actions and other requests from a licensee or potential licensee rather 
than nonbinding generic milestone schedule guidelines. These deadlines 
include taking no more than 18 months to make a final decision on an 
application to construct and operate a new reactor of any type and 
taking no more than one year to make a final decision on an application 
to continue operating an existing reactor of any type. Section 5(a) 
also directs the NRC to adopt shorter deadlines tailored to particular 
reactor types or licensing pathways as appropriate. In addition, 
section 5(e) of the E.O. directs the NRC to establish a process for 
high-volume licensing of microreactors and modular reactors, and 
section 5(d) of the E.O. directs the NRC to establish an expedited 
pathway to approve reactor designs that the DOW or the DOE have tested 
and that have demonstrated the ability to function safely.
    In some cases, completing licensing decisions within the E.O.-
directed timeframes could turn on timely completion of a contested 
adjudication. However, the Commission's existing hearing procedures in 
title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) part 2, ``Agency 
Rules of Practice and Procedure,'' provide model milestones that would 
collectively exceed the timeframes specified in E.O. 14300. And these 
milestones, which are not binding, are sometimes exceeded in practice. 
Therefore, the Commission is revising its hearing procedures to support 
faster adjudications that will enable the agency to meet the licensing 
timelines contemplated by the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300. The NRC 
believes that the revised adjudicatory deadlines will provide 
reasonable timeframes for parties to meaningfully raise, and the 
presiding officer to resolve, disputed issues. These revisions will 
continue the overall trend, described previously, of reducing the 
formality in NRC adjudications to enhance efficiency.
    The NRC's predecessor agency, the Atomic Energy Commission, at one 
time believed that the AEA required formal adjudicatory hearings in all 
cases (2004 Adjudications Rule, 69 FR 2182, page 2183, January 14, 
2004). Now the prevailing view is that, with the exception of hearings 
on applications for licenses to construct and operate

[[Page 69448]]

uranium enrichment facilities, informal hearings will also satisfy the 
AEA. (2004 Adjudications Rule, 69 FR 2182, pages 2183 through 2186, 
January 14, 2004). On balance, these amendments generally use simpler, 
more informal processes and shorter schedules to complete adjudications 
within the timeframes contemplated in the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 
14300.While the final rule establishes three primary pathways for 
hearings (a ``Standard Proceeding'' for 18-month reviews, a ``Focused 
Proceeding'' for 12-month proceedings, and an ``Expedited Proceeding'' 
for faster reviews), the Commission does not intend for these 
designations to be rigid. Rather, in light of the direction in E.O. 
14300 to ``adopt shorter deadlines tailored to particular reactor types 
or licensing pathways as appropriate,'' the rule does not preclude 
reliance on the Commission's authority to move a proceeding to a faster 
pathway when warranted. Additionally, within the pathways, the final 
rule directs the presiding officer to ensure the hearing schedule does 
not exceed the staff review schedule to the greatest extent 
practicable. Collectively, these provisions should ensure that the 
hearing procedures for each adjudication appropriately reflect the 
complexity of the issues raised by the underlying application.
    The Commission has chosen to use a Licensing Board as the default 
presiding officer for contested licensing proceedings, including 
license transfers, because Boards are independent and statutorily 
established, possess legal and technical expertise, and are well placed 
to efficiently conduct NRC licensing proceedings given their experience 
and ability to focus exclusively on adjudicatory matters. Considering 
the wide variety of situations a Board could face after a contention is 
admitted, the presiding officer will have considerable flexibility to 
select the appropriate procedures for resolving disputed issues within 
the strict timeframes imposed by this rulemaking. For example, these 
procedures will continue to rely primarily on written pleadings and 
statements to maintain clarity and precision in the record, although 
the presiding officer will have the flexibility to convene oral 
proceedings when necessary.
    These revisions will require evidentiary hearings to be held as 
soon as practicable after a decision admitting contentions. 
Nonetheless, to support more efficient and timely resolution of 
admitted contentions in certain circumstances, the procedures and 
practice will still provide for motions to dismiss contentions and 
motions for summary disposition prior to an evidentiary hearing.
    These procedures also address new or amended contentions filed 
later in the NRC's review process to ensure that the NRC is still able 
to complete adjudications in a timely manner. The Commission is making 
three significant revisions to accomplish this goal.
    First, in light of the dynamic nature of our licensing process, 
parties frequently file new or amended contentions throughout NRC 
adjudications, often in response to amended applications or other new 
information. To accommodate these filings within the 18-month and 1-
year E.O. 14300 timelines, the revisions establish deadlines the 
presiding officer must use in setting hearing schedules that will 
provide sufficient time to (1) fully litigate an initial round of 
contentions (including an evidentiary hearing on any admitted 
contentions) and (2) fully litigate a second round of new or amended 
contentions through an evidentiary hearing on those contentions, even 
if there is no overlap between the rounds of litigation.
    Second, the Commission recognizes that, in rare instances, critical 
issues could arise sufficiently late in a proceeding to challenge the 
E.O. 14300 timelines for a decision on the application. To ensure that 
only critical issues have the potential to be admitted late in the 
proceeding, these revisions establish that the NRC's standards for 
reopening the record will apply to contentions raising new issues that 
are submitted after the date by which the presiding officer would be 
expected to enter an initial decision after an evidentiary hearing on 
the initial round of contentions, assuming that the evidentiary hearing 
phase immediately commences upon the admission of the contention and 
there are no delays along the way.
    Third, these revisions establish that new or amended contentions 
would not be considered pending before the agency until the presiding 
officer finds there is good cause for submitting these contentions 
after the prescribed initial filing deadline for contentions (i.e., 
that they have been timely submitted based on new, materially different 
information). This change will, as discussed later in this notice, 
eliminate the possibility of parties delaying licensing in certain 
proceedings simply by filing an untimely new or amended contention.
    As stated previously, the Commission is establishing hearing 
schedules that would allow for two non-overlapping hearings to be 
conducted within the 18-month and 1-year E.O. 14300 timelines--one 
hearing for contentions submitted by the initial filing deadline for 
contentions and a second hearing held thereafter on a new or amended 
contention arising later in the review. The revisions to 10 CFR part 2 
primarily accomplish this acceleration by requiring the presiding 
officer to commence the evidentiary hearing as soon as practicable 
after admitting contentions. In contrast, evidentiary hearings 
generally do not begin under the existing rules until after the staff 
completes its review.
    This change also reflects the Commission's understanding that the 
E.O.'s discussion of fixed deadlines for the NRC's evaluation to 
support a final decision on the application refers to the agency's 
approval of the licensing action or other request if the NRC's 
evaluation determines that applicable requirements are met. Given this 
understanding, the changes in this final rule focus on ensuring that 
there is a final presiding officer decision on all contested issues 
within the E.O. 14300 timelines as these decisions have immediate 
effect by default, regardless of the pendency of appeals. As such, the 
presiding officer's decision would allow the licensing decision to be 
made even in circumstances where the AEA requires a hearing to be 
completed before the issuance and effectiveness of a license. 
Consequently, in this final rule, the appeals process occurs outside of 
the scope of the fixed deadlines outlined in section 5(a) of E.O. 
14300. Nonetheless, the NRC is streamlining the appeals process to 
support the overarching goals of the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300. First, 
this final rule makes small changes to the filing deadlines for 
appeals, shortening the process. Second, the Commission recognizes the 
importance of issuing its adjudicatory decisions in a timely manner and 
will use milestones in its internal procedures to effectuate this goal.
    While the Commission expects these revisions will substantially 
improve the efficiency of NRC contested licensing adjudications, they 
do not constitute a wholesale rewrite of 10 CFR part 2, and many 
proceedings such as enforcement proceedings, proceedings on denials of 
applications, or proceedings for construction or operation of a high-
level waste geological repository are only minimally impacted. 
Proceedings under Sec.  52.103 or 53.1452 are also minimally impacted 
by the changes because the procedures for such hearings are established 
by case-specific order, and the NRC will consider modifications to the 
existing standard procedures for these proceedings in a separate 
process. Further, a final rule published April 15,

[[Page 69449]]

2026 (91 FR 20063) increased flexibility in the mandatory hearing 
process, and a policy statement published June 8, 2026 (91 FR 34661) 
made changes to the agency's mandatory hearing process for reactors to 
increase efficiency and timeliness while also enhancing public 
participation. Additionally, in a separate rulemaking, the NRC proposed 
changes to the agency's implementation of the National Environmental 
Policy Act (91 FR 42086, July 7, 2026), which could impact the scope of 
issues that may be permissible for adjudication in contested hearings. 
The changes in this final rule are a series of targeted amendments 
intended to ensure timely and efficient contested adjudication for most 
NRC licensing actions.
    This final rule reflects changes to the proposed rule made in 
response to public comments, as documented in the ``NRC Response to 
Public Comments: Streamlining Contested Adjudications in Licensing 
Proceedings'' (hereafter, Comment Response Document). This final rule 
also accounts for changes made to the regulations since publication of 
the proposed rule, including a final rule adding a new 10 CFR part 53, 
``Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for Advanced 
Reactors'' (91 FR 15696, March 30, 2026), which generally revised 10 
CFR part 2 to apply the same processes to applications under 10 CFR 
part 53, ``Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for 
Commercial Nuclear Plants,'' as would apply to corresponding 
applications under 10 CFR part 50, ``Domestic Licensing of Production 
and Utilization Facilities,'' or 10 CFR part 52, ``Licenses, 
Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants.'' This final 
contested hearings rule includes these changes and consistently treats 
10 CFR part 53 applications and licenses the same as the corresponding 
applications and licenses under 10 CFR parts 50 and 52. This final rule 
also accounts for changes made by the rule, mentioned previously, that 
increased flexibility in the mandatory hearing process (91 FR 20063, 
April 15, 2026). In addition, this final rule makes certain 
corrections, clarifications, and other minor changes that were not in 
response to comments but that the NRC identified during the development 
of the final rule. All changes made in the final rule logically grow 
out of the proposed rule provisions.

III. Discussion

    To achieve the objectives described previously, the Commission is 
amending 10 CFR part 2 in the following areas:

Hearing Schedule Framework and New Definitions in 10 CFR 2.4

    In this rule, the NRC is taking a tailored approach to timeframes 
for hearing requests and evidentiary hearings to account for specific 
types of applications rather than the one-size-fits-all approach in the 
existing regulations, where the same time is generally provided for 
hearing requests and evidentiary hearings on shorter or simpler 
applications as on longer or complex applications. The tailored 
timeframes in this final rule provide sufficient time for the parties 
to meaningfully raise and litigate disputed issues in the type of 
proceeding at issue and for the presiding officer to make accurate 
determinations on these disputed issues. Using tailored hearing 
timelines is consistent with direction in the Nuclear Energy Innovation 
and Modernization Act section 102(c), ADVANCE Act section 504, and E.O. 
14300 section 5 regarding specified timelines for different types of 
NRC reviews.
    To accomplish this objective, the NRC is establishing three basic 
timeframes for most licensing proceedings so that the NRC's hearing 
regulations are clear and manageable and provide greater flexibility, 
while recognizing that it would be impractical to establish a multitude 
of timeframes for every type of proceeding and constantly modify 
hearing processes and regulations to account for the different NRC 
decision-making schedules as they are updated over time. Nonetheless, 
as discussed later, the NRC is accounting for potential variability in 
NRC decision-making schedules by requiring the presiding officer in 
each proceeding to establish a hearing schedule that, to the greatest 
extent practicable, will not extend past the NRC staff's scheduled date 
for completing its review of the application. This provision could, for 
example, address an expedited NRC review under E.O. 14300 section 5(d) 
of a reactor design tested and demonstrated by DOE or DOW.
    The NRC is adding new definitions in Sec.  2.4 to account for the 
three basic timeframes established by this rule. The new definitions 
are ``Standard Proceeding,'' ``Focused Proceeding,'' and ``Expedited 
Proceeding,'' where Standard Proceedings have the longest hearing 
schedules, Expedited Proceedings have the shortest hearing schedules, 
and Focused Proceedings have hearing schedules in between these two 
categories. The proposed rule followed the same basic scheduling 
construct as this final rule but did not establish formal labels for 
Standard Proceedings or Focused Proceedings.\4\ The NRC has determined 
that the clarity of 10 CFR part 2 will be enhanced by formal labels for 
each basic type of proceeding, and the final rule is accordingly adding 
definitions for Standard Proceedings and Focused Proceedings. Also, in 
establishing the basic hearing timeframes in this rule, the NRC has 
followed the general approach taken in the proposed rule by specifying 
the applications that are in the Standard Proceeding category and the 
applications that are in the Expedited Proceeding, with the Focused 
Proceeding category including, with certain limited exceptions, all 
other licensing proceedings.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \4\ The preamble for the proposed rule (91 FR 10450, March 3, 
2026) referred to Standard Proceedings as ``most complex'' 
proceedings, referred to Focused Proceedings as ``other'' 
proceedings, and referred to Expedited Proceedings as ``highly 
expedited proceedings.''
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The new definition for ``Standard Proceeding'' captures those 
applications that generally present more complex technical issues than 
those applications that fall into the other categories. While the 
applications in this category are not all equally complex, they are 
currently subject to the longer 18-month standard NRC review schedules 
and warrant longer hearing schedules because of the anticipated 
complexity of material on which contentions could be based, as well as 
the potential complexity of the technical issues that could be the 
subject of admitted contentions. As discussed later in this notice, the 
hearing schedules established for Standard Proceedings support the 
potential completion of two non-overlapping evidentiary hearings within 
13.5 months and allow for Commission consideration of any associated 
appeals within 18 months.
    Reactor applications falling under the Standard Proceeding category 
are those for the grant of a construction permit, an operating license, 
or a combined license under 10 CFR part 50, 52, or 53 for a commercial 
production or utilization facility (other than a non-power production 
or utilization facility (NPUF)), where the application does not 
reference an NRC approval providing finality in the adjudicatory 
proceeding on design matters (e.g., a design certification or 
manufacturing license).\5\

[[Page 69450]]

For materials licenses, the proposed rule applied the Standard hearing 
schedules to the following licenses: (1) a license to construct and 
operate a uranium enrichment facility, and (2) a license to construct 
or operate a uranium recovery or fuel cycle facility under 10 CFR part 
40, ``Domestic Licensing of Source Material,'' or part 70, ``Domestic 
Licensing of Special Nuclear Material.'' The NRC is retaining these 
categories in the final rule but in response to comments is clarifying 
what constitutes a ``fuel cycle facility'' in this category. 
Specifically, licenses for new fuel cycle facilities that are subject 
to the Standard hearing schedules are those that are subject to subpart 
H of 10 CFR part 70, ``Additional Requirements for Certain Licensees 
Authorized To Possess a Critical Mass of Special Nuclear Material,'' 
i.e., a facility with a critical mass of special nuclear material that 
necessitates an integrated safety analysis and other requirements in 
subpart H because of the facility's safety significance. In addition, 
in this final rule, the NRC has determined that an application for a 
new low-level-waste disposal facility under 10 CFR part 61, ``Licensing 
Requirements for Land Disposal of Radioactive Waste,'' should be 
included in the Standard Proceeding category. The currently operating 
low-level waste disposal facilities are licensed by agreement states 
rather than the NRC, but it is possible that an application for a new 
facility might be filed with the NRC. If such an application were to be 
filed, the NRC has determined that the application should be included 
in the Standard Proceeding category given the types of technical issues 
that would be involved.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \5\ The proposed rule specifically referenced a design 
certification and manufacturing license on the basis that these NRC 
approvals provide finality in the adjudicatory proceeding on design 
matters. To be consistent with the language used in proposed Sec.  
2.1207(c) (final Sec.  2.1207(b)), the final rule adjusts the 
proposed rule Sec.  2.309(b) language to focus on the function that 
the NRC approval provides (e.g., providing finality in the 
adjudicatory proceeding on design matters), with a design 
certification and manufacturing license being given as examples of 
approvals that provide such finality. A similar adjustment is made 
to the language of final rule Sec.  2.1207(a).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The new definition for ``Focused Proceeding'' covers those 
applications that are subject to more focused NRC reviews because they 
are generally less complex than applications within the Standard 
Proceeding category. As such, Focused Proceedings are amenable to 
faster NRC reviews and hearing schedules than those reserved for 
Standard Proceedings. Many applications in the Focused Proceeding 
category are currently subject to a 12-month standard NRC review 
schedule. Several others are subject to an 18-month standard NRC review 
schedule, but the NRC would aim to complete the review of these 
applications more quickly than 18 months if practical since they would 
generally be less complex and narrower in scope than other applications 
subject to an 18-month standard review schedule (e.g., 10 CFR part 52 
combined license applications referencing a design certification). 
Appropriately accelerating hearing schedules, when warranted, for 
limited scope applications responds to direction in E.O. 14300, section 
5(a), which states that the E.O. 14300 deadlines are ``maximum time 
periods,'' and that ``the NRC shall adopt shorter deadlines tailored to 
particular reactor types or licensing pathways as appropriate.'' As 
discussed later in this notice, the hearing schedules established for 
Focused Proceedings support the potential completion of two non-
overlapping evidentiary hearings within 12 months.
    Following the approach taken in the proposed rule, the Focused 
Proceeding category has been defined to include all proceedings for the 
grant, renewal, licensee-initiated amendment, or termination of 
licenses or permits subject to 10 CFR parts 30, 32 through 36, 39, 40, 
50, 52, 53, 54, 55, 61, 70, and 72, except for a Standard Proceeding, 
an Expedited Proceeding, a proceeding for the construction or operation 
of a high-level waste geological repository, or a proceeding on a 
denial of an application. Applications in the Focused Proceeding 
category include, but are not limited to, operating reactor license 
renewal applications under 10 CFR part 53 or 54; applications for new 
10 CFR part 50, 52, or 53 licenses referencing an NRC approval 
providing finality in the adjudicatory proceeding on design matters 
(e.g., a design certification or manufacturing license); 10 CFR part 52 
or 53 early site permit applications; materials license renewal 
applications; applications to construct or operate new facilities under 
10 CFR part 70 that are not subject to the requirements of subpart H of 
10 CFR part 70; license amendment requests; NPUF license applications; 
and limited work authorization applications. Moreover, several 
commenters proposed accelerating Nth-of-a-kind proceedings. The 
Commission expects that the agency will seek to complete these 
proceedings significantly in advance of the E.O. 14300 timeframe 
because the staff will have previously resolved the majority of 
technical issues. Moreover, the NRC recently finalized a new reactor 
generic environmental impact statement, which will resolve a 
significant number of environmental issues in most Nth-of-a-kind 
proceedings. Therefore, the NRC has also added these proceedings to the 
Focused Proceedings hearing track. Additionally, commenters noted that 
faster proceedings would be appropriate for uranium enrichment 
facilities that employ technologies that have been licensed and 
operated. The NRC agrees. Given the limited set of technical and 
environmental contentions these proceedings are expected to raise, the 
NRC has also added these proceedings to the definition of Focused 
Proceedings.
    Similarly, several commenters suggested providing faster procedures 
for limited work authorizations. Generally, these proceedings only 
resolve a limited set of technical and siting issues. Moreover, while 
in the past a limited work authorization may have occasioned a more 
detailed environmental review, the NRC recently finalized a generic 
environmental impact statement for new reactors that would resolve the 
majority of these issues in most cases. Consequently, the NRC has also 
included proceedings on these applications within the definition of 
``Focused Proceedings.''
    The new definition of ``Expedited Proceeding'' captures those 
applications that are particularly simple or narrow in scope and should 
be subject to significantly expedited hearing schedules because they 
will be reviewed on a more expedited basis than the other reviews the 
NRC would typically handle. As reflected in the standard review 
schedules on the NRC website at 
https://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/generic-schedules.html
, the NRC currently intends to apply an 18-month or 12-
month review schedule to most types of applications it receives. 
However, some applications have a significantly shorter anticipated 
review schedule. For example, measurement uncertainty recapture uprate 
license amendments currently have a six-month review schedule, stretch 
power uprates have a nine-month review schedule, and amendments 
adopting a Technical Specifications Task Force traveler using the 
Consolidated Line-Item Improvement Process currently have a seven-month 
review schedule. To support expedited decision-making on these 
applications, the NRC is including these three types of applications 
within the definition of ``Expedited Proceeding,'' and applying 
significantly expedited hearing schedules to these proceedings to 
reflect the shorter review schedules and focused nature of these 
reviews. Additionally, several commenters noted that licensing 
applications that reference prior NRC approvals providing issue 
finality are not likely to spark complex litigation.

[[Page 69451]]

The NRC agrees that these proceedings would present a sufficiently 
narrowed set of issues, particularly when the application references a 
categorical exclusion, that Expedited Proceedings would be warranted in 
all cases. Applications taking advantage of issue finality and 
categorical exclusions will have the vast majority of technical and 
environmental issues resolved for the facility, and the remaining 
issues are unlikely to present complex contentions requiring extended 
litigation. Therefore, the NRC has revised the definition ``Expedited 
Proceedings'' to always include these types of applications. As 
discussed later in this notice, the hearing schedules established for 
Expedited Proceedings support the potential completion of an 
evidentiary hearing within 5 to 5.5 months.
    The NRC recognizes that other applications may warrant more 
expedited treatment in the hearing process than would otherwise apply 
given the definitions discussed previously. For example, in accordance 
with E.O. 14300 section 5(e), the NRC has published a proposed rule (91 
FR 23628, May 1, 2026) to establish a risk-informed and performance-
based regulatory framework in a new 10 CFR part 57 for rapid licensing 
and high-volume deployment of new microreactors and other reactors with 
comparable risk profiles. As part of that rulemaking, the NRC has 
included a specific request for comment on whether to include certain 
10 CFR part 57 applications within the ``Expedited Proceeding'' 
category.
    Independent of these efforts, the NRC might later decide to include 
an application or a class of applications within the scope of 
``Expedited Proceeding'' without changes to the Code of Federal 
Regulations. The NRC already has the authority to impose or modify 
hearing procedures and schedules without changes to the Code of Federal 
Regulations and has done so in the past (e.g., through case-specific 
orders for uranium enrichment proceedings). To enhance the NRC's 
agility to expedite proceedings in appropriate circumstances, the 
Commission may use its authority to determine whether a specific 
application or class of applications should be included in a different 
hearing timeline. One commenter pointed out that it would not be 
appropriate for microreactor applications to impose hearing schedules 
patterned on 18-month NRC reviews of applications to construct and/or 
operate larger, complex reactors. As discussed in the Comment Response 
Document, the NRC agrees with the commenter on this point, but the term 
``microreactor'' is not precisely defined and the NRC has not defined, 
and has not proposed to define, in the regulations a category of 
smaller commercial reactors licensed under 10 CFR part 50, 52, or 53 
that would be subject to more accelerated hearing schedules and 
processes than larger commercial reactors licensed under the same 
frameworks. The issue of defining the category of entities that would 
be considered ``microreactors'' in 10 CFR parts 50, 52, and 53 is 
outside the scope of this rulemaking.
    The definitions of ``Standard Proceeding,'' ``Focused Proceeding,'' 
and ``Expedited Proceeding'' cover most, but not all, license-related 
proceedings before the NRC. These definitions do not include 
enforcement proceedings, proceedings on denials of applications, 
proceedings for construction or operation of a high-level waste 
geological repository, or proceedings under Sec.  52.103 or 53.1452 
because this rule is not intended to establish schedules for such 
proceedings. In addition, these definitions do not cover license 
transfer proceedings because the NRC is taking a more nuanced approach 
to transfer proceeding schedules, as explained later in this notice, 
while remaining generally consistent with the schedule timeframes 
established by this rule.
    In sum, these changes would support hearing schedules that align 
with the overall timeliness goals of E.O. 14300, including the 18-month 
and 1-year deadlines for certain licensing actions, with more expedited 
hearing schedules for certain applications when warranted.
    Finally, the NRC is adding a new definition of ``Standard Hearing 
Completion Date'' to Sec.  2.4 to support changes elsewhere in this 
notice regarding standards and schedules for late-stage challenges 
after the deadline. As discussed later, the NRC considers it 
appropriate in certain cases to apply a faster evidentiary hearing 
schedule to such challenges if the associated contention is admitted 
for hearing. In addition, the NRC considers it appropriate to apply the 
reopening criteria to such challenges that raise new issues not within 
the scope of existing admitted or proposed contentions. The NRC is 
applying these provisions after the point in the proceeding in which 
the NRC could have completed an evidentiary hearing in the situation 
where a contention filed by the hearing request deadline is both 
admitted for hearing and proceeds to the evidentiary hearing phase 
immediately after the admission of the contention, consistent with the 
NRC's policy of holding evidentiary hearings as early as practicable. 
Because the revised regulations define the time (1) in which 
contentions, answers, and replies are to be filed, (2) when decisions 
on contention admissibility are due, and (3) when initial decisions 
after an evidentiary hearing are to be issued, the NRC is able to 
compute the Standard Hearing Completion Date for different types of 
proceedings. The NRC is including the Standard Hearing Completion Dates 
for these proceedings in Sec.  2.1207 and in Federal Register notices 
announcing an opportunity to request a hearing, as discussed later in 
this notice. The definition of ``Standard Hearing Completion Date'' in 
Sec.  2.4 defines how the date is calculated, consistent with the 
description in this paragraph.
    The proposed rule used the term ``Standard Record Closure Date'' 
rather than ``Standard Hearing Completion Date,'' but the NRC changed 
the terminology in this final rule to reflect that the ``Date'' is used 
for two independent purposes: to identify a time after which certain 
evidentiary hearing schedules are accelerated and to define a time when 
proposed contentions raising new issues must meet the standards for 
reopening the record. The NRC also revised the proposed rule definition 
so that it focuses solely on how the Standard Hearing Completion Date 
is calculated, with provisions on reopening appearing solely in Sec.  
2.326.

Other Changes to Definitions in Sec.  2.4

    The NRC is also changing the definitions of ``contested 
proceeding'' and ``potential party'' in Sec.  2.4, which are related to 
matters discussed in more detail later in this notice. The NRC is 
modifying the definition of ``contested proceeding'' to conform to 
changes to Sec.  2.309(c) regarding motions for leave to file hearing 
requests, intervention petitions, and contentions after the deadline 
established for such submissions (collectively ``challenges after the 
deadline''), in particular to reflect that until the motion for leave 
to file is granted upon a showing of good cause, the challenge after 
the deadline would not be considered pending before the NRC. 
Nonetheless, while the challenge after the deadline is not pending 
before the NRC, the motion for leave to file would still be considered 
within the scope of the contested proceeding since the purpose of the 
motion is to seek permission to file a challenge after the deadline to 
contest the application. The NRC is also revising the definition of 
``potential

[[Page 69452]]

party'' by removing references to subpart M of 10 CFR part 2, 
``Procedures for Hearings on License Transfer Applications,'' which 
currently governs proceedings on license transfer applications. Many 
recent license transfer applications raise technical issues on 
decommissioning the Commission did not intend subpart M to address. 
Therefore, the NRC is eliminating subpart M and conducting license 
transfer proceedings under the more general provisions in subpart L of 
10 CFR part 2, ``Simplified Hearing Procedures for NRC Adjudications.''

Representation by Those Who Are Not Attorneys

    For the reasons given in the Comment Response Document, the NRC has 
not adopted the limitations on non-attorney representation that were 
included in the proposed rule. Also, as discussed in a 2020 decision in 
the Vogtle proceeding (CLI-20-6, 91 NRC 225), the Commission has given 
greater latitude to hearing requests submitted by non-attorney 
intervenors while acknowledging that non-attorney petitioners are still 
expected to comply with our procedural rules. The NRC is clarifying 
that it is retaining this latitude for non-attorneys; however, this 
latitude is limited to construing the pleadings.

Requirements for Publication of Federal Register Notices Announcing an 
Opportunity To Request a Hearing, and Petition To Intervene

    The NRC is making several changes to the regulations in Sec. Sec.  
2.101, 2.104, and 2.105 regarding the publication of Federal Register 
notices announcing an opportunity to request a hearing and petition to 
intervene. First, the NRC will generally notice these hearing 
opportunities as early as practicable. The hearing process may not 
reasonably be initiated before the NRC staff accepts the application 
for review (i.e., dockets the application), but noticing the hearing 
opportunity as early as practicable thereafter would accelerate issue 
identification and resolution and could help mitigate any unavoidable 
delays that may occur later (e.g., from illness of counsel or a 
witness). For certain proceedings, Sec.  2.104(a) already requires the 
staff to issue the hearing notice ``as soon as practicable after the 
NRC has docketed the application.'' With one exception, the NRC is 
changing Sec. Sec.  2.104 and 2.105 to expand this requirement to 
publish notices as soon as practicable to other Federal Register 
notices announcing a hearing opportunity in order to accelerate the 
initiation of the adjudicatory process, with a conforming change to 
Sec.  2.101(f)(5). The exception pertains to notices of proposed action 
subject to the requirements of Sec.  50.91 or 53.1515. Notices under 
Sec.  50.91 or 53.1515 are for proposed amendments to specified 
production and utilization facility licenses. Historically, such 
notices have generally been published on a periodic basis given their 
volume. Given the high volume, it would not be practical to require 
individual Federal Register notices for these licensing actions. Also, 
only a small number of these amendments are challenged in the hearing 
process, and the associated licensing actions may be taken during the 
pendency of a hearing if the NRC makes a final no significant hazards 
consideration determination.
    Second, the NRC is modifying Sec. Sec.  2.104 and 2.105 to provide 
that Federal Register notices announcing a hearing opportunity must 
provide additional clarity by stating the Standard Hearing Completion 
Date specified in Sec.  2.1207 and the additional filing deadline 
information required by Sec.  2.309(b)(5). The basis for this change is 
described later in this notice in the context of changes to Sec.  2.309 
requirements for hearing requests, intervention petitions, and 
contentions.
    Consistent with current practice, Federal Register notices will 
continue to state that prospective participants should notify the 
Secretary at least 10 days before filing a hearing request. While the 
agency recognizes this practice as helpful, in that it provides 
sufficient time to create an electronic hearing docket for a proceeding 
to facilitate compliance with electronic filing requirements and 
identify applicant and NRC staff contacts, imposing the practice as an 
additional requirement, as requested by one commenter on the rule, is 
not necessary. Outside the rulemaking process, the NRC will look to 
clarify notice templates to highlight the importance of meeting the 
requirements for electronic filing, including a timely request to 
establish a docket.

Good Cause for Extensions of Time

    Meeting the licensing deadlines contemplated in the ADVANCE Act and 
E.O. 14300 will require strict adherence to the schedules described in 
the rule. Under existing Sec.  2.307(a), time periods in 10 CFR part 2 
may be extended either upon a showing of good cause or by stipulation 
of the parties. An extension of time by stipulation of the parties 
usually does not result in significant delay as the applicant and NRC 
staff have an interest in timely adjudication, and such extensions 
sometimes lead to more efficient resolution of issues (e.g., an 
extension to complete consultation on a motion). However, contested 
extensions are more likely to lead to delay, and in recent years the 
NRC has sometimes found good cause for extensions based on requests 
detailing ordinary circumstances, such as general resource planning 
challenges.
    The NRC has determined that no changes must be made to Sec.  
2.307(a), but in order to ensure that extension requests do not 
undermine timely adjudications, the NRC is reiterating the need for 
parties to clearly demonstrate good cause under Sec.  2.307. Good cause 
is necessarily context specific, and the Commission has previously 
explained in its 2012 rule (77 FR 46562, August 3, 2012) that good 
cause in the context of Sec.  2.307 should include ``extraordinary 
circumstances.'' Extraordinary circumstances are those events that are 
not within the parties' control, such as sickness or weather. Major 
holidays could similarly be an extraordinary circumstance. Thus, in 
normal circumstances the presiding officer should only grant an 
extension when a circumstance outside of the ordinary occurs that is 
not brought on by the movant's actions or inactions. In addition, under 
the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300, efficient and timely decision-making on 
license applications is a key focus area for the agency. Therefore, in 
circumstances where an extension request has the potential to extend an 
adjudicatory proceeding past the NRC staff's scheduled date to complete 
its review, the presiding officer should take into account schedule 
needs when making its determination and minimize the amount of time 
necessary to accommodate the circumstances giving rise to good cause.

Requirements for Hearing Requests, Intervention Petitions, and 
Contentions

    The NRC is revising its regulations for hearing requests, 
intervention petitions, and contentions to (1) refine but not raise the 
contention admissibility criteria, (2) accelerate filing and decision 
deadlines consistent with the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300, (3) clarify 
and improve the requirements for hearing requests, intervention 
petitions, and new or amended contentions filed after the deadline in 
Sec.  2.309(b) (i.e., ``challenges after the deadline''), and (4) 
provide clarity to participants on timelines, including when the 
reopening standards would apply to contentions raising new issues after 
the Standard Hearing Completion Date. However, as discussed in the 
Comment Response Document, this final rule is not adopting a provision 
in the proposed rule that would have

[[Page 69453]]

bifurcated filings and decisions on standing and contention 
admissibility (with standing being addressed on a more accelerated 
schedule), nor is the final rule adopting proposed Sec.  2.309(k), 
which would have accelerated the filing of merits information on 
proposed contentions. As such, this final rule will not change current 
practice on these two matters: litigants will continue to address 
standing and contention admissibility in the same filings, the 
presiding officer will address both matters in the same decision, and 
litigants will not be required to file additional information on the 
merits of proposed contentions.
    The NRC is also refining the contention admissibility criteria in 
two ways. First, the NRC is augmenting the requirement in Sec.  
2.309(f)(1)(iv) to demonstrate that a contention is material by 
requiring the petitioner to specify the legal requirement on which the 
contention is based. Specifying the pertinent legal requirement is 
important for demonstrating the materiality of the contention, and 
clarity in this regard can avoid needless confusion about the legal 
basis for a contention (e.g., safety versus environmental requirements) 
and the inefficiencies that accompany efforts to resolve such 
confusion. Second, the NRC is revising Sec.  2.309(f)(1)(vi) to require 
the petitioner to clearly indicate whether a contention is one of 
omission or adequacy. Different requirements apply to contentions of 
omission versus contentions of adequacy, and a lack of clarity 
regarding the nature of the contention requires additional resources 
from the NRC staff, applicant, and presiding officers to address.
    As discussed previously, the NRC is taking a tailored approach to 
timeframes for initial filings and decisions thereon to account for 
specific types of applications rather than the more one-size-fits-all 
approach in the existing regulations, where the same time is provided 
for contentions on shorter or simpler applications as on longer or more 
complex applications. These tailored timeframes provide sufficient time 
for petitioners to meaningfully raise disputed issues in their hearing 
requests, for the applicant and NRC staff to file answers to hearing 
requests, and for the presiding officer to determine whether the 
standing and contention requirements are met.

paragraph, this final rule includes the following schedules for hearing

 Under revised Sec.  2.309(b), hearing requests and 
intervention petitions are due within set time periods after 
publication of the Federal Register notice announcing the hearing 
opportunity, depending on the type of application. As reflected in

period for Standard Proceedings, retaining the existing 20-day filing

 The NRC is retaining the existing 60-day filing period for 
hearing requests in Standard Proceedings because the pertinent 
applications generally present more complex technical issues than other

 The NRC is establishing a 45-day filing period for hearing

generally less complex than applications within the Standard Proceeding

 The NRC is providing a 30-day hearing request period for

    The NRC is making several modifications to Sec.  2.309(c) to 
clarify and improve the requirements for challenges after the deadline 
(i.e., hearing requests, intervention petitions, and new or amended 
contentions filed after the deadline in Sec.  2.309(b)). First, the NRC 
is clarifying and revising its regulations to avoid delays in making 
licensing decisions in certain proceedings due to the submission of 
challenges after the deadline that arrive near the end of the NRC 
staff's application review. Currently, petitioners must submit 
``motions for leave to file'' contentions after the deadline that must 
satisfy Sec.  2.309(c). Hearing requests and intervention petitions 
after the deadline must also satisfy Sec.  2.309(c), although NRC 
regulations do not require a ``motion for leave to file'' such filings. 
The NRC is extending the ``motion for leave to file'' concept to 
hearing requests and intervention petitions after the deadline, and 
clarifying that challenges after the deadline would not be considered 
pending before the NRC until the motion for leave to file has been 
granted upon a showing of good cause under Sec.  2.309(c). These 
changes address statutory requirements for a pre-effectiveness hearing 
(or pre-effectiveness hearing opportunity) for certain licensing 
actions.\7\ For example, AEA section 189a.(1)(A) allows the NRC to 
issue operating licenses for certain facilities ``in the absence'' of a 
request for hearing from a person whose interest may be affected; 
therefore, the pendency of a hearing request before the NRC could 
affect the timing of the NRC's licensing decision. However, the AEA 
does not require a hearing request submitted after the specified 
deadline for hearing requests to be considered automatically pending 
before the NRC regardless of when it was filed. Rather, the related AEA 
section 189a.(1)(A) requirement specifying a 30-day notice period for 
operating licenses indicates that Congress contemplated that hearing 
requests be filed within specified periods.\8\ The AEA provides no 
absolute right to file challenges after the specified notice period, 
nor does it indicate that petitioners may file challenges at any time 
they choose and thereby delay NRC action on the application. Under this 
change, challenges after the deadline would not be considered pending 
before the agency (and therefore would not delay NRC action on an 
application subject to a pre-effectiveness hearing requirement) unless 
and until the motion for leave to file the challenge after the deadline 
has been granted upon a showing under Sec.  2.309(c) of good cause for 
filing after the deadline. Thus, as reflected in a new Sec.  
2.309(c)(7) and in revisions to Sec.  2.340(i)(2), (j)(4), and (k)(2), 
the mere submission of such challenges after the deadline would not 
interfere with timely NRC licensing or regulatory decisions, even for 
those applications subject to a pre-effectiveness hearing (or pre-
effectiveness hearing opportunity) requirement. The effectiveness of 
the licensing action in these circumstances would be stayed only if the 
petitioner meets the standard for granting a stay request.\9\ To 
reflect the motion for leave to file terminology, the NRC is also 
making conforming changes in other paragraphs of Sec.  2.309 and in 
Sec. Sec.  2.4 (definition of ``contested proceeding'') and 2.323(a).

Selection of Hearing Procedures

    As a result of this final rule, the NRC will use a revised hearing 
format in subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 to govern the adjudication of 
admitted contentions in almost all proceedings for the grant, renewal, 
licensee-initiated amendment, termination, or transfer of licenses or 
permits subject to 10 CFR parts 30, 32 through 36, 39, 40, 50, 52, 53, 
54, 55, 61, 70 and 72. Subpart L is already used for most of these 
proceedings, but the NRC is increasing its use of subpart L with the 
following changes:

 The NRC will conduct proceedings on a license to construct 
and operate a uranium enrichment facility under subpart L of 10 CFR 
part 2 rather than subpart G of 10 CFR part 2 because the revised 
subpart L provides a faster, more streamlined process than subpart G 
and is better suited for licensing proceedings (in fact, most licensing 
proceedings are already conducted under subpart L). The NRC previously 
decided to conduct these uranium enrichment proceedings under subpart G 
because AEA section 193 requires such proceedings to be conducted ``on

Reopening Standards

    The NRC intends to complete contested hearings on a schedule that 
supports licensing within the timelines contemplated by the ADVANCE Act 
and E.O. 14300. Consequently, to ensure that the adjudicatory process 
concludes within these timelines, the revised adjudicatory procedures 
have been constructed so as to generally accommodate an evidentiary 
hearing on admitted contentions filed by the Sec.  2.309(b) deadline 
for filing contentions and a hearing on admitted contentions filed 
after that deadline, even if there is essentially no overlap between 
the filing and decision schedules for the two. To help accomplish this, 
the rule introduces a mechanism referred to as the Standard Hearing 
Completion Date, which facilitates the timely disposition of issues 
during the contested hearing process. The Standard Hearing Completion 
Date serves an important dual purpose in maintaining efficiency by 
identifying a time after which certain evidentiary hearing schedules 
are accelerated and, as discussed in the following paragraphs, defining 
a time when proposed contentions raising new issues must meet the 
standards for reopening the record.
    The NRC acknowledges that in rare cases critical issues may arise 
late in a proceeding that might require the adjudication to exceed the 
NRC staff review timelines established in accordance with the ADVANCE 
Act and E.O. 14300. However, only critical issues should lead to such 
delays. Existing Sec.  2.326 addresses this in part by requiring 
contentions filed after the record closes for an adjudicatory 
proceeding to meet the heightened reopening standards in Sec.  2.326, 
which require the contention to be timely in accordance with Sec.  
2.309(c), address a significant safety or environmental issue, and 
demonstrate that it would likely materially affect the outcome of the 
proceeding. Under existing case law, the reopening standards would 
apply after the last live contention in the proceeding is resolved.
    However, it is possible under existing precedent for a chain of 
periodically

[[Page 69457]]

filed new or amended contentions, none of them admissible, to hold open 
the record of the proceeding even to the end of the NRC's review of an 
application. To avoid this anomalous result and to provide a standard 
time for when the record would close to new issues for a proceeding, 
the revisions to Sec.  2.326 add a new paragraph (e)(1) stating that 
the record for the proceeding will automatically close at the Standard 
Hearing Completion Date, a date providing sufficient time to hold an 
evidentiary hearing on admitted contentions submitted by the original 
deadline. The Standard Hearing Completion Date is based on the timeline 
structure of a particular proceeding, and applying the reopening 
standards to new issues raised after this date balances the rights of 
potential intervenors with the need for efficiency and predictability 
in a proceeding. The imposition of the reopening standards at this 
juncture in the timeline is intended to ensure that new issues 
submitted late in the proceeding are only admitted if shown to be 
critical, and would not affect litigation of issues already raised in a 
previously filed contention, as explained in subsequent paragraphs.
    There may be instances in which an evidentiary hearing is completed 
before the Standard Hearing Completion Date. Consistent with existing 
practice, the presiding officer is expected to issue an order closing 
the record after the evidentiary hearing and before issuing the initial 
decision. In keeping with existing practice and consistent with themes 
underlying existing agency case law, Sec.  2.326(e)(1) also provides 
that the record closes for the adjudicatory proceeding if the presiding 
officer enters an order closing the record following an evidentiary 
hearing but before the Standard Hearing Completion Date.
    These revisions to Sec.  2.326 comport with existing NRC precedent 
and are not intended to supersede the concepts already enshrined in 
case law. The Commission has routinely emphasized that the adjudicatory 
record for a proceeding closes at the conclusion of an evidentiary 
hearing, for example, in a 2012 decision in the Pilgrim proceeding 
(CLI-12-3, 75 NRC 132). Also, the Commission has applied the reopening 
provisions even earlier in a proceeding (e.g., when a proceeding 
terminates once all contentions have been decided), such as in the 
Commission's 2012 decision in the North Anna proceeding (CLI-12-14, 75 
NRC 692). Therefore, under existing precedent, the proceeding would 
terminate and the reopening provisions would apply in a situation when 
a presiding officer denies all hearing requests filed by the deadline 
in Sec.  2.309(b) and there are no pending contentions in the 
proceeding.
    The Commission has also recognized that if some issues are pending 
once the record closes, the record may remain open on those limited 
issues; an example is the Commission's decision in the Pilgrim 
proceeding (CLI-12-3, 75 NRC 132). This practice of keeping the record 
open for particular issues while closing the overall record for the 
proceeding has been supported in federal court in a 2013 decision in 
Massachusetts v. NRC (708 F.3d 63, footnote 18). Therefore, the new 
Sec.  2.326(e)(1) also clarifies that if other contentions either 
remain pending or are subject to a motion for leave to file at the time 
the record closes, the record will remain open only with respect to the 
particular issues raised by those contentions. As a result, petitioners 
could continue to litigate live contentions filed prior to closure of 
the record under final Sec.  2.326(e)(1) without having to meet the 
reopening standards. This would include (in certain narrow cases) 
filing proposed amendments of contentions on issues within the scope of 
the existing contention. For example, a petitioner may adjust an 
environmental contention filed on the application to address an NRC 
environmental document's discussion of the same particular issue, given 
that the NRC has the ultimate responsibility to comply with 
environmental laws and (when the NRC environmental document has been 
issued) the hearing on the issue would concern the adequacy of the NRC 
environmental document. Similarly, the reopening standards under final 
Sec.  2.326(e)(1) would not apply to a contention of adequacy arising 
from new information mooting a contention of omission, where the 
contention of adequacy remains within the bounds of the bases set forth 
in support of the original contention. This aligns with well-
established scope principles outlined in existing caselaw, such as the 
McGuire/Catawba proceeding (CLI-02-28, 56 NRC 373). However, reopening 
would apply to a new or amended contention filed after the record 
closure date under Sec.  2.326(e)(1) that is not squarely within the 
confines of a live contention filed before that date (e.g., if the pre-
record-closure contention raised a particular environmental 
qualification concern for a component, a post-record-closure contention 
would have to meet the reopening standards if it raised a different 
type of environmental qualification concern for the component).
    By providing the public with an opportunity to request a hearing 
prior to closing the record, this change comports with applicable 
Federal case law considering challenges to the NRC's reopening 
standards. In the 1984 decision Deukmejian v. NRC (751 F.2d 1287), the 
U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit addressed a challenge to the 
NRC requiring an intervenor to meet the reopening standards to 
participate in a proceeding on a full power operating license in order 
to challenge an applicant's application to amend a low power license by 
extending the license term. The court determined the two actions were 
separate proceedings. By requiring the petitioner to meet the 
heightened pleading requirements in the reopening standard, the NRC 
improperly abridged the petitioner's hearing rights under section 189a. 
of the Atomic Energy Act. Thus, under Deukmejian, the NRC must provide 
petitioners with at least one opportunity to participate in an 
adjudication prior to closing the record. The revisions to Sec.  2.326 
meet this standard because they would not close the record until well 
after the opportunity to request a hearing expires.
    Also, because the revisions to Sec.  2.326 close the record in the 
specified circumstances, the NRC is revising Sec. Sec.  2.104, 2.105, 
and 2.309(b)(5) to require Federal Register notices announcing 
opportunities to request hearings to state the Standard Hearing 
Completion Date for the proceeding. This will put the public on notice 
and provide additional clarity on record closure.
    Further, to avoid any implication that final Sec.  2.326(e)(1) 
overrides or otherwise annuls existing case law, the NRC is adding in 
response to comments a new Sec.  2.326(e)(2) clarifying that, if the 
presiding officer enters an order closing the record following 
resolution of all live contentions in the proceeding, the record for 
the adjudicatory proceeding will close on the date specified in the 
order.
    Finally, in addition to the adjustments described previously to 
address the scheduling directives of the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300, 
the agency is modifying the criteria included in Sec.  2.326(a)(2) to 
state that a significant environmental issue under the National 
Environmental Policy Act can only be identified in a proceeding where a 
categorical exclusion listed in 10 CFR part 51 does not apply. The 
final rule language clarifies that categorical exclusions specifically 
pertain to the agency's obligations under the National Environmental 
Policy Act. In circumstances where a categorical

[[Page 69458]]

exclusion is used to comply with the National Environmental Policy Act, 
by definition, there are no significant environmental issues associated 
with the proposed Federal action under that statute. The agency 
considers this to be a clarity change responsive to the potential for 
increased use of categorical exclusions in future reviews. In another

Discovery

    The NRC is making several changes to reduce burdens to the parties 
from their obligations to make certain disclosures after contentions 
are admitted in most licensing proceedings and is also expediting the 
production of initial disclosures to support the accelerated 
evidentiary hearing timeframes in subpart L of 10 CFR part 2.\10\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \10\ These changes do not affect the discovery provisions in 
proceedings under subpart G or subpart J of 10 CFR part 2.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The NRC staff's hearing file obligations are being entirely 
eliminated by this rule. Experience shows the hearing file currently 
required by Sec.  2.1203 is burdensome and provides little value to the 
litigation because it covers the entire application under review 
instead of focusing on the admitted contentions. Moreover, the hearing 
file was established before the NRC required electronic filing of 
applications, regularly posted the entirety of applications and related 
documents on its website, and developed robust search functions in 
public-facing ADAMS. To the extent members of the public face 
difficulties in searching ADAMS, NRC Public Document Room staff are 
available to assist during business hours. Thus, the rationale 
supporting the hearing file obligation has become outdated. While the 
NRC is eliminating the hearing file requirements in Sec.  2.1203, it is 
retaining paragraph (d) of this section, which specifies that no 
additional forms of discovery are authorized beyond what is permitted 
by subpart C of 10 CFR part 2.
    In a change from the proposed rule, the NRC is retaining the NRC 
staff's Sec.  2.336(b) disclosure obligations. While the staff's 
disclosures largely replicate the applicant's required disclosures or 
otherwise concern internal documents that are typically not produced to 
the other parties, there could be cases where the staff would disclose 
relevant information that would not otherwise be produced.
    To effectuate the elimination of the hearing file requirement, the 
NRC is changing the scope of case-specific orders issued under Sec.  
2.307(c) for access to sensitive unclassified information. Under 
existing Commission precedent, these orders no longer apply to a 
petitioner if its hearing request is granted, as discussed in a 2010 
decision in the South Texas Project combined license proceeding (CLI-
10-24; 72 NRC 451, 461-63). That precedent, however, was issued when 
regulations required the NRC staff to disclose documents unrelated to 
the admitted contentions. Since the NRC staff would no longer produce a 
hearing file under Sec.  2.1203, a change is needed so that a 
petitioner who is admitted as a party could continue to make requests 
for access under the Sec.  2.307(c) access order on matters outside the 
scope of disclosures under Sec.  2.336. The NRC intends to revise its 
templates for Sec.  2.307(c) access orders to reflect this change; no 
change to the regulations is needed for this purpose.
    The NRC is modifying the Sec.  2.336(b) disclosures obligation in 
proceedings on denials of applications. In these types of proceedings, 
the staff is required to be a party and is in opposition to the 
applicant. The NRC is modifying Sec.  2.336(b) to tailor the required 
document disclosures to the circumstances associated with a proceeding 
on a denial of an application (e.g., the document categories associated 
with the application and NRC correspondence with the applicant would 
not apply because the applicant already would be in possession of this 
material). Finally, the NRC is making conforming changes to Sec.  
2.336(a) to reflect applicant disclosures in a proceeding on a denial 
of an application.
    Second, the NRC is further modifying Sec.  2.336 to reduce the 
burdens of other participants. Parties commonly agree to exclude from 
disclosures non-public draft documents that have not been circulated 
among the parties; the NRC is codifying this practice in the NRC's 
regulations in new subparagraphs (a)(4) and (b)(2). Moreover, in 
response to comments, the NRC is adding new subparagraphs (a)(5) and 
(b)(3) to exclude internal instant messages, text messages, and voice 
messages from mandatory disclosure absent a showing of exceptional 
circumstances. This exclusion only applies to communications that are 
internal to a party, its litigation team, and its contractors; if a 
single external person or entity is included in a communication, the 
communication would not be subject to this exclusion. These internal 
communications are generally high-volume, but low-value, and similar to 
non-public drafts that reveal a party's internal thinking. Generally, 
NRC licensing proceedings involve admitted contentions from qualified 
intervenors and focus on the technical conclusions on safety and 
environmental issues and how they are supported,\11\ rather than on 
intent or motive that could be revealed through a party's internal 
thinking. Therefore, the NRC finds it appropriate to focus disclosures 
on technical documents that will reach the ultimate issues in dispute. 
However, to avoid inadvertently excluding relevant technical documents 
merely because they are attached to an excluded internal communication, 
the NRC is not excluding any documents attached to those excluded 
internal communications. These attachments would need to be included 
within the scope of mandatory disclosures if they are relevant to the 
admitted contentions. Also, in exceptional circumstances, such as when 
an admitted contention or license denial proceeding relates to a 
party's intent or motive and these types of internal communications 
would be relevant to the specific issue in the proceeding, the 
presiding officer may require that these communications be included.
