Conforming Changes to Scheduling Regulations

    To accommodate the shorter timeframes for completing adjudications 
contemplated by this final rule, the NRC is making a number of 
conforming amendments to other sections in 10 CFR part 2, which pertain 
to scheduling. Specifically, the NRC is revising paragraph (b) in Sec.  
2.312, ``Notice of hearing,'' to reflect the Commission's expectation 
that considerations informing the selection of a time and place for a 
hearing should not override the overall timeframes established for 
timely adjudications by this rule or by any proceeding-specific 
Commission order. To provide additional flexibilities that may 
facilitate meeting those timeframes, the NRC is also revising Sec.  
2.329, ``Prehearing conference,'' to give the presiding officer or 
Commission discretion on whether to hold a prehearing conference.
    Next, the NRC is making a number of edits to Sec.  2.332, ``General 
case scheduling and management,'' to conform to the streamlined 
procedures and shortened timeframes elsewhere in this rule. Because the 
timeframes in this rule are mandatory, the NRC is revising paragraph 
(a) to reflect the presiding officer's obligation to develop a schedule 
that would meet the licensing timeframes in this rule. Likewise, the 
NRC is amending paragraph (d) to conform to the Commission's 
expectations that hearings under subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 would 
ordinarily begin once the presiding officer admits contentions, not 
when the staff issues its review documents. Specifically, the presiding 
officer would immediately proceed to an evidentiary hearing after the 
admission of a contention unless either (i) the NRC staff or applicant 
intend to seek dismissal or summary disposition of the admitted 
contention or (ii) the NRC staff decides to participate as a party but 
is not yet able to take final positions on the matters in controversy. 
Section 2.332(d) includes notification requirements to effectuate this 
provision--the proposed rule required these notifications within seven 
days of admission of the contention, but to avoid unnecessary delay, 
this final rule requires the notifications to be filed as soon as 
possible and no later than seven days after admission of the 
contention. The commencement of the evidentiary hearing phase would be 
delayed in cases where the NRC staff or applicant seek to resolve a 
contention through a motion to dismiss or a motion for summary 
disposition because the process for seeking dismissal or summary 
disposition is quicker and less resource-intensive than an evidentiary 
hearing; thus, the dismissal or summary disposition process may be a 
more efficient way of resolving a contention if the presiding officer 
decides that the standards for dismissing the contention are 
satisfied.\13\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \13\ The exception for summary disposition has been added to 
this final rule in response to comments; the proposed rule referred 
only to motions to dismiss. This change is a modest expansion of the 
proposed rule provision that is consistent with its stated purpose 
(91 FR 10462) of providing for contention resolution processes that 
are ``quicker and less resource-intensive than an evidentiary 
hearing[.]'' As the proposed rule recognized (91 FR 10464), 
``Summary disposition may be a useful tool to avoid the resource 
expenditures associated with an evidentiary hearing.''
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The other reason for delaying the commencement of the evidentiary 
hearing--when the NRC staff seeks to participate as a party but is not 
able to take a final position on the matters in controversy--reflects 
the special role the NRC staff has in the licensing process and the 
Commission's desire to ensure that the presiding officer is aware of 
the NRC staff's considered position on the contested issues in those 
cases where the staff chooses to participate as a party. The NRC staff 
may not always be in the position (particularly early in its review of 
an application-specific or first-of-a-kind issue) to take a final 
position on the matters in controversy (e.g., the NRC staff is seeking 
further information from the applicant or further considering 
information already provided). In this regard, the NRC staff is in a 
different position from the petitioner (who formulated and supported 
the proposed contention and should be in a position to commence the 
evidentiary hearing upon admission of the contention) and the applicant 
(who developed the application and should have the wherewithal to 
promptly address challenges to it). In the interest of prompt 
adjudication, revised Sec.  2.332(d) further requires the NRC staff, in 
cases where it decides to participate as a party but is not yet able to 
take a final position on the admitted contention, to prioritize its 
resources to put itself in a position to provide testimony on the 
contention at the earliest practicable time and notify the presiding 
officer and the other parties when the staff is ready to do so.
    Because the evidentiary hearing phase would, with certain 
exceptions, immediately commence after admission of a contention, 
litigants should ensure they are prepared to move immediately to an 
evidentiary hearing posture if a proposed contention is admitted. Thus, 
the NRC expects that litigants will consider their potential strategies 
and resource needs to litigate contentions at an evidentiary hearing 
before a presiding officer issues its decision on contention 
admissibility.
    Section 2.332(d) is further revised to require the presiding 
officer, to the greatest extent practicable, to establish a schedule 
that will not extend past the

decision-making when it is practicable to do so and is intended to 
address both individual NRC reviews that are on a more expedited review

proceedings rather than model milestones.

the standard in Sec.  2.307(a) for extending a schedule and to 
incorporate an ``extraordinary circumstances'' standard for extending

Revisions to Hearing Format in Subpart L of 10 CFR Part 2 and 
Conforming Changes Elsewhere in Part 2

    As explained previously, the NRC is making a number of significant 
changes to subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 to streamline and accelerate the 
hearing process for proceedings for the grant, renewal, licensee-
initiated amendment, termination, or transfer of licenses or permits 
subject to 10 CFR parts 30, 32 through 36, 39, 40, 50, 52, 53, 54, 55, 
61, 70 and 72. The two most significant changes are (1) to establish 
strict deadlines for the issuance of initial decisions in most 
licensing proceedings and (2) to provide greater flexibility to the 
presiding officer to decide which components of the subpart L hearing 
process are needed to support the presiding officer's decision-making. 
The NRC is also making other changes to streamline proceedings and 
ensure prompt and accurate decision-making, as discussed in the 
following paragraphs.
    The NRC is establishing strict deadlines for the issuance of an 
initial decision to ensure that adjudicatory proceedings are promptly 
conducted to support the efficiency goals of the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 
14300. These deadlines are tailored to different types of proceedings 
to account for the varying complexity of different license applications 
as well as the greater need for expedited decision-making in certain 
proceedings (e.g., in Expedited Proceedings). These deadlines may only 
be extended if extraordinary circumstances necessitate a delay.
    The NRC is also providing presiding officers greater flexibility in 
structuring the subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 evidentiary hearing phase 
because admitted contentions could take a wide variety of forms, and 
the presiding officer in an individual proceeding is better placed to 
decide what information is needed for the admitted contentions before 
it to support accurate decision-making and the development of a sound 
record, while ensuring that the parties are given a fair and equal 
opportunity to make their cases (e.g., if one party may file written 
testimony and a position statement, all other parties would have the 
same opportunity). The presiding officer would also tailor the hearing 
schedule to the particular circumstances of a proceeding while 
complying with requirements for decision-making deadlines.
    The specific changes to subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 and conforming 
changes elsewhere in this part are detailed in the following 
subsections for clarity and completeness.
A. Changes to Scope Provisions in Sec.  2.1200
    The NRC is revising Sec.  2.1200 to reflect the modified scope of 
subpart L of 10 CFR part 2, as discussed previously in the context of 
changes to Sec. Sec.  2.310 and 2.700. As stated before, license 
transfer proceedings will now be conducted under subpart L, as well as 
contested proceedings on the grant of licenses to construct and operate 
uranium enrichment facilities. The NRC is also clarifying Sec.  2.1200 
to reflect the existing provision in Sec.  2.310(b) providing that 
enforcement proceedings may be held under subpart L if all parties 
agree.
B. Changes to Sec.  2.1202 Regarding the NRC Staff's Authority and Role
    The NRC is making several modifications to the provisions in Sec.  
2.1202 regarding the NRC staff's authority to take licensing actions 
and its role in the adjudicatory proceeding. First, the NRC is 
modifying provisions on the issuance and effectiveness of licensing 
decisions during the pendency of a hearing. Currently, Sec.  2.1202(a) 
provides that the NRC staff is expected to promptly issue its approval 
or denial of the application, or take other appropriate action on the 
underlying regulatory matter for which a hearing was provided, and that 
the NRC staff's action is effective upon issuance except for several 
listed licensing actions. The NRC is revising the list of exceptions in 
Sec.  2.1202(a) as follows:

 Currently, the listed exceptions include all applications 
to construct and/or operate a production or utilization facility 
(including limited work authorizations and combined licenses). However, 
the pre-effectiveness hearing requirements in AEA section 189a. apply 
to production and utilization facilities licensed under AEA sections 
103 and 104b. (corresponding to facilities under Sec. Sec.  50.21(b) 
and 50.22 and 10 CFR part 53) or testing facilities licensed under AEA 
section104c. (corresponding to a facility under Sec.  50.21(c) that 
meets the definition of ``testing facility'' in Sec.  50.2). The AEA's 
pre-effectiveness hearing requirements do not apply to production and 
utilization facilities licensed under AEA section104a. (i.e., medical 
therapy facilities under Sec.  50.21(a)) or to production and 
utilization facilities licensed under AEA section 104c. that are not 
testing facilities (i.e., non-testing facilities under Sec.  50.21(c)). 
The NRC is revising Sec.  2.1202(a)(1) to reflect the scope of the 
AEA's pre-effectiveness

[[Page 69461]]

hearing requirements and in recognition of the lower safety 
significance of medical therapy facilities under Sec.  50.21(a) and 
non-testing facilities under Sec.  50.21(c).

 The NRC is revising Sec.  2.1202(a)(3) to remove the 
existing exception for 10 CFR part 52 or 53 manufacturing licenses and 
put in its place an exception for licenses to construct and operate 
uranium enrichment facilities. In the 2007 rule adding the exception 
for manufacturing licenses (72 FR 49352, page 49420, August 28, 2007), 
the Commission acknowledged that there is no statutory requirement for 
including an exception for manufacturing licenses, but stated, 
``Nonetheless, as a matter of discretion, the NRC has decided to treat 
manufacturing licenses similar to construction permits in this regard, 
although the NRC reserves the right to change its practice in the 
future.'' The NRC is removing the exception for manufacturing licenses 
because such licenses are not subject to the AEA's pre-effectiveness 
hearing requirements, a manufacturing license authorizes only the 
manufacture (not operation) of a facility, and vendors may fabricate 
major portions of a facility without a manufacturing license so long as 
those portions do not constitute a production or utilization facility. 
In these circumstances, there is no substantial reason to delay the 
issuance and effectiveness of a manufacturing license because of a 
pending hearing on the license application. The NRC is including an 
exception for applications for licenses to construct and operate 
uranium enrichment facilities. Such applications are currently subject 
to hearings under subpart G of 10 CFR part 2, but the NRC will now 
conduct contested hearings on these applications under subpart L of 10 
CFR part 2. As stated previously, licenses to construct and operate 
uranium enrichment facilities are subject to a statutory pre-
effectiveness hearing requirement, so it is appropriate to include them 
in the list of exceptions in Sec.  2.1202(a).
    The NRC is also modifying Sec.  2.1202(b), regarding the role of 
the NRC staff in the hearing process, to accelerate the time in which 
the NRC staff is required to notify the presiding officer and the other 
parties of whether it will participate as a party in the proceeding, 
consistent with changes being made to Sec.  2.332(d).
C. Changes to Sec.  2.1203 Regarding Elimination of Hearing File
    As discussed previously, the NRC is eliminating the hearing file 
requirements in paragraphs (a) to (c) of Sec.  2.1203, while retaining 
the prohibition on additional discovery currently in paragraph (d) of 
Sec.  2.1203.
D. Changes to Sec.  2.1205 Regarding Summary Disposition
    The NRC is making several changes regarding the schedule for 
summary disposition motions. First, to avoid unduly burdening parties 
as they undertake evidentiary hearing activities, the NRC is modifying 
Sec.  2.1205(a) so that summary disposition motions are not permitted 
later than 30 days before the scheduled date for filing initial written 
testimony, absent permission from the Commission or presiding officer. 
Summary disposition may be a useful tool to avoid the resource 
expenditures associated with an evidentiary hearing, but after 
evidentiary hearing activities are underway, the filing of summary 
disposition motions risks distracting parties from their hearing 
preparations and burdening them unnecessarily.
    Second, consistent with other changes in this final rule, the NRC 
is reducing the time for filing answers to summary disposition motions 
from 20 days to 15 days after service of the motion. The NRC also is 
providing a 20-day period from the filing of answers for a decision on 
the motion. Fifteen days should be sufficient for parties to address 
the pertinent standards for summary disposition motions, and a 20-day 
period for decisions is consistent with the overall hearing schedule 
and other timeframes for decisions in this final rule.
E. Changes to Sec.  2.1206 to Sec.  2.1210 Regarding the Hearing 
Process and Schedule
    Currently, Sec.  2.1206 to Sec.  2.1210 provide the principal 
requirements for the subpart L evidentiary hearing process and 
schedule, including prescriptive requirements for which written filings 
are permitted and when, and whether an oral hearing must be held. For 
the reasons discussed earlier, the NRC is replacing these detailed 
requirements with simpler, more flexible, and more informal provisions 
for most proceedings. However, as reflected in an amended Sec.  
2.1206(a)(2), a hearing in a proceeding expressly required by the AEA 
to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing 
(i.e., a proceeding for the grant of a license to construct and operate 
a uranium enrichment facility) will be required to comply with the 
APA's formal procedures for ``on the record'' hearings.\14\ As 
explained in the following paragraphs, Sec. Sec.  2.1206 and 2.1207 are 
completely revised, while Sec. Sec.  2.1208 and 2.1209 are removed and 
reserved, and minor conforming changes are made to Sec.  2.1210.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \14\ In the final rule, the NRC has modified this provision in 
Sec.  2.1206(a)(2) and the related provision in Sec.  2.1206(d) to 
refer to ``a proceeding expressly required by the [AEA] to be 
determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing'' 
rather than to a proceeding on a license to construct and operate a 
uranium enrichment facility. Although a proceeding on a license to 
construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility is the only NRC 
licensing proceeding subject to the ``on the record'' procedures, 
the NRC made the change to focus on the underlying statutory 
requirement, which will also account for any potential future 
statutory changes without the need for a revision to the 
regulations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Under revised Sec.  2.1206(a), the presiding officer would issue a 
scheduling order that would include the presiding officer's 
determinations on which written filings are permitted, the schedule for 
these filings, whether to hold an oral hearing, and the schedule for 
issuing an initial decision. Motions for cross-examination under Sec.  
2.1204 would be permitted (consistent with the existing regulations). 
Otherwise, the presiding officer would largely have flexibility to 
decide which written filings the parties would be permitted to make to 
provide the information necessary to support the presiding officer's 
decision. These potential written filings, which are listed in Sec.  
2.1206(b)(1), are (1) initial testimony, position statements, and 
supporting exhibits; (2) rebuttal testimony, position statements, and 
supporting exhibits; (3) motions in limine and motions to strike; (4) 
written briefing and/or written responses to questions from the 
presiding officer; (5) proposed questions for the presiding officer to 
ask the witnesses; and (6) proposed findings of fact and conclusions of 
law. These listed filings are currently available in a hearing process 
under subpart L of 10 CFR part 2, but the presiding officer would have 
flexibility to determine which filings to permit in a particular case. 
Similarly, the presiding officer would generally have flexibility to 
determine whether an oral hearing is needed to support the presiding 
officer's decision--currently, an oral hearing is required unless all 
parties agree to a hearing based solely on written presentations, but 
the NRC sees no need to require that an oral hearing be held as a 
default matter in all proceedings.
    The initial decision is the culmination of the evidentiary hearing 
process, and the NRC is requiring that the scheduling order include the 
schedule for an initial decision, which must comply with the 
requirements of Sec. Sec.  2.332 and (if applicable) 2.1207. As 
discussed later in this document, the amended Sec.  2.1207

[[Page 69462]]

provides schedule requirements for the issuance of initial decisions in 
most licensing proceedings.
    Revised Sec.  2.1206(b)(2) identifies certain additional 
flexibilities for the parties and the presiding officer that would 
apply depending on which written filings are permitted. Historically, 
written testimony in subpart L proceedings has been submitted in 
question-and-answer form, but a party would be allowed to submit 
testimony in affidavit form if the party prefers. Section 2.1206(b)(2) 
also provides that if statements of position and proposed findings of 
fact and conclusions of law are both permitted, parties would be 
allowed to file statements of position in the form of proposed findings 
and conclusions to facilitate the prompt preparation of proposed 
findings and conclusions after the hearing. Finally, Sec.  2.1206(b)(2) 
clarifies the presiding officer's authority to allow oral motions in 
limine or motions to strike in lieu of (or in addition to) written 
filings. The amended Sec.  2.1206(b)(2) does not provide an exhaustive 
list of flexibilities, and the presiding officer retains all authority 
provided in the pertinent provisions of 10 CFR part 2 to regulate the 
conduct of the proceeding.
    The amended Sec.  2.1206(c) retains requirements in existing 
subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 regarding the participants' ability to 
designate and present their own witnesses; the presiding officer's 
discretion to formulate and ask questions as the presiding officer 
considers appropriate; the presiding officer's authority to address 
situations where a witness is unable to appear in an oral hearing; and 
existing provisions on the propounding of questions by the presiding 
officer and the submission of proposed questions for the presiding 
officer to ask the witnesses.
    While the presiding officer would ordinarily have great flexibility 
to structure the evidentiary hearing, for two types of proceedings--a 
proceeding expressly required by the AEA to be determined on the record 
after opportunity for an agency hearing (i.e., a proceeding on an 
application to construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility) and 
a proceeding on a denial of an application--revised Sec.  2.1206(d) 
requires (consistent with existing subpart L of 10 CFR part 2) that (1) 
a transcribed oral hearing be held unless all parties jointly agree to 
dispense with an oral hearing, and (2) each party be permitted to file 
written testimony, a position statement, and supporting exhibits; to 
submit rebuttal evidence and argument; and to file proposed findings of 
fact and conclusions of law. These elements of an evidentiary hearing 
are required for a proceeding concerning the grant of a license to 
construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility to maintain 
consistency with the requirements for formal ``on the record'' hearings 
in the APA.\15\ The NRC is also retaining these elements of a subpart L 
hearing for denials of applications because hearings on denials 
ordinarily arise from a ``demand for hearing'' under Sec.  2.103 or 
2.108 that would not typically involve the robust issue development 
provided in the initial filings under the Sec.  2.309 process.\16\

    \15\ The NRC recognizes that an oral hearing may not be required

may, in ``applications for initial licenses . . . , when a party

2.108(b), any person whose interest may be affected may file an

    The NRC is providing scheduling requirements in Sec.  2.1207 for 
issuance of initial decisions in proceedings under subpart L, with the 
exception of enforcement proceedings and proceedings on denials of 
applications.\17\ For each type of proceeding, Sec.  2.1207 includes 
(1) a deadline for initial decisions for contentions, including (as 
applicable) a shorter deadline for initial decisions on contentions 
submitted after the Standard Hearing Completion Date, (2) a 
specification of the Standard Hearing Completion Date for that type of 
proceeding, and (3) a requirement that extraordinary circumstances are 
necessary for delays beyond the deadline for initial decision. 
Deadlines are stated in terms of calendar days from the admission of 
the contention, assuming that the presiding officer immediately 
proceeds to an evidentiary hearing in accordance with Sec.  2.332(d), 
although if this does not occur (e.g., the NRC staff is not yet able to 
take a final position on the contested issues, the applicant seeks to 
resolve the admitted contention through a summary disposition motion) 
the deadline would run from an alternative triggering event established 
in the scheduling order (e.g., the NRC staff's notification that it is 
able to take a final position on the contested issues, a presiding 
officer order denying or partially denying an applicant summary 
disposition motion).Also, in accordance with changes to Sec.  2.334(c) 
discussed previously, the presiding officer must provide written 
notification to the Commission any time during the course of the 
proceeding when it appears that the issuance of the initial decision 
will be delayed beyond the time specified in the hearing schedule.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \17\ The NRC is not imposing specific schedules for issuance of 
initial decisions in subpart L enforcement proceedings and 
proceedings on denials of application because circumstances are 
likely to vary in these proceedings. In addition, neither the

general requirement in Sec.  2.332(c) to establish a schedule to 
expedite the proceeding, and the Commission expects that presiding 
officers would consider relevant comparable hearing schedules in 
Sec.  2.1207 in establishing a hearing process and schedule that 
ensure a prompt and fair proceeding that supports accurate decision-
making and development of an adequate record.

    In establishing deadlines, the NRC considered the anticipated 
complexity of the pertinent application, along with associated NRC 
review deadlines and goals. More time is given for the Standard 
Proceeding applications subject to an 18-month standard NRC review 
schedule, while less time is given for less complex applications. While 
the complexity of the issues admitted for hearing in a particular 
proceeding will depend on case-specific factors, more complex 
applications have the potential for more complex contested issues, 
which is a factor to be considered in establishing these general 
evidentiary hearing deadlines in the regulations. However, if a less 
complex dispute is amenable to a shorter process, the Licensing Board 
should account for that in its schedule for an individual proceeding.
    In some cases, the NRC has not established a standard review 
schedule shorter than 18 months for a particular application, but the 
NRC would seek to come to a final decision in substantially less than 
18 months, if practical, because the application review is less 
complicated or of narrower scope (e.g., a 10 CFR part 52 commercial 
reactor application referencing an issued design certification, which 
finally resolves most design issues for both the staff review and the 
adjudicatory proceeding). The deadlines in final Sec.  2.1207 account 
for these circumstances.
    The NRC has also considered different timelines depending on when 
the contention was submitted. For two reasons, the NRC is generally 
establishing a shorter deadline for initial decisions on contentions 
submitted after the Standard Hearing Completion Date. First, an 
expedited schedule is needed for admitted contentions submitted later 
in a proceeding to support prompt NRC decision-making consistent with 
the

[[Page 69463]]

direction in the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300. As stated previously and 
discussed in more detail later in the context of table 4, the NRC's 
general overall goal with these changes has been to establish a process 
where two non-overlapping hearings could be held within the 18-month 
and 1-year E.O. 14300 deadlines (one hearing on contentions submitted 
by the Sec.  2.309(b) deadline--as reflected in the calculation of the 
Standard Hearing Completion Date--and the second hearing on a new or 
amended contention submitted after the Standard Hearing Completion 
Date). Second, consistent with other changes to 10 CFR part 2 in this 
final rule (in particular, those in Sec.  2.332(d)), the NRC would 
ordinarily proceed to an evidentiary hearing on contentions submitted 
earlier in the proceeding as soon as practicable. Thus, hearings on 
admitted contentions submitted later in the proceeding would be 
expected to narrowly focus on new information arising later in the 
review, in contrast to contentions submitted early in the review that 
might embrace the entire application. To promote clarity, Sec.  2.1207 
specifies the Standard Hearing Completion Date for different types of 
proceedings, based on the new definition of this term in Sec.  2.4, and 
the Standard Hearing Completion Date for a particular proceeding would 
be specified in the Federal Register notice announcing the hearing 
opportunity, in accordance with this rule's revisions to Sec. Sec.  
2.104, 2.105, and 2.309. The Standard Hearing Completion Dates in this 
final rule reflect changes to proposed rule scheduling provisions 
discussed elsewhere in this notice; also, the NRC has corrected an 
omission in the proposed rule by including a separate Standard Hearing 
Completion Date in final Sec.  2.1207(d) for transfer proceedings other 
than those for a license authorizing operation of a reactor.

Appeals

    As discussed previously, in this final rule, the appeals process 
occurs outside of the scope of the fixed deadlines outlined in section 
5(a) of E.O. 14300 because the appeals process does not itself delay 
the issuance or effectiveness of a license. Nonetheless, the NRC is 
promulgating broad changes to its contested hearing process, including 
revisions associated with appeals, in response to the ADVANCE Act and 
the general direction to streamline the public hearings process in 
section 5(j) of E.O.14300. To streamline the overall process, the 
changes to the appeals process primarily implement shortened timelines. 
Further, simple structural changes were made in Sec.  2.311 to 
streamline the requirements and add clarity. These changes involve 
consolidation of the requirements in the section into paragraph (a), 
Types of appeals covered under this section; paragraph (b), Timing of 
appeals and associated filings under this section; and paragraph (c), 
Scope of appeals under this section. These structural changes primarily 
involve consolidating existing Sec.  2.311(d) into Sec.  2.311(c) and 
consolidating existing Sec.  2.311(e) into Sec.  2.311(a), (b), and 
(c). The following paragraphs discuss the NRC's streamlining of the 
appeals process.
    Specifically, the agency is amending Sec.  2.341(b)(1) to reduce 
the time for filing a petition for review of an agency decision with 
the Commission from 25 days to within 20 days after service of a full 
or partial initial decision by a presiding officer, and within 20 days 
after service of any other decision or action by a presiding officer 
with respect to which a petition for review is authorized. Sections 
2.311 and 2.341(b)(3) are amended to allow any other party to the 
proceeding to file an answer supporting or opposing Commission review 
within 20 days after service of a petition for review and reduce the 
period of time the petitioning party has to file a 5-page reply brief 
from 10 days to 7 days. In response to public comments, the page limit 
count for answers to appeals in Sec.  2.341(b)(3) is adjusted from 25 
pages to 30 pages. This adjustment matches the page limit count allowed 
for petitions for review, promoting equity and consistency in the 
regulations. The modest reductions in filing times described previously 
are in keeping with the ADVANCE Act and the direction of E.O. 14300 to 
streamline processes. For interlocutory appeals under Sec.  
2.311(a)(1)-(3), the agency is limiting the time for filing the appeal 
or petition from 25 days to 20 days, consistent with the other appeals.
    For interlocutory appeals under Sec.  2.311(a)(1)-(3) and petitions 
for interlocutory review under Sec.  2.341(f)(2), the agency makes no 
procedural distinction between them and other appeals because, in many 
cases, the complexity of an interlocutory appeal is similar to other 
appeals. Also, this final rule modifies Sec.  2.311 to add a reply 
brief opportunity for interlocutory appeals under Sec.  2.311(a)(1)-
(3).
    The agency is modifying Sec.  2.311(b)(2), which addresses 
interlocutory appeals of an order under Sec.  2.310 selecting hearing 
procedures, to require the moving party to file an appeal with the 
Commission no later than seven days after the order--this should be 
sufficient time to address the comparatively simple matter of selection 
of hearing procedures. The NRC similarly allots seven days after 
service of the appeal for any party to file a brief in opposition. The 
regulatory language further clarifies that a reply brief in response to 
a brief in opposition is not permitted.
    The proposed rule had proposed changes to Sec.  2.311 to address 
interlocutory appeals of decisions on contentions submitted by the 
deadline in Sec.  2.309(b) but separately from the hearing request to 
account for the proposed rule's bifurcation of standing and contention 
admissibility. Since the final rule does not adopt the proposed rule's 
bifurcation scheme, these changes have not been included in the final 
rule.

Referred Rulings and Certified Questions

    In cases where the presiding officer identifies significant and 
novel legal or policy issues, or where prompt decision by the 
Commission is necessary to materially advance the orderly disposition 
of the proceeding, the presiding officer has the discretion to refer 
its ruling to the Commission or certify a question to the Commission 
for disposition. To ensure efficiency in this process, the agency is 
including language in Sec.  2.323(f)(1) clarifying that where 
practicable, the presiding officer should first rule on the matter in 
question and then seek Commission input in the form of a referred 
ruling, rather than certify a question to the Commission without 
issuing a ruling. This change aims to minimize delays in the proceeding 
during the pendency of the Commission's review. Section 2.323(g) is 
adapted to clarify that unless otherwise ordered, the referral of a 
ruling to the Commission does not stay the proceeding or extend the 
time for performance of any act.

Reconsideration

    To shorten the process for motions for reconsideration in keeping 
with the streamlining and burden reduction efforts of the ADVANCE Act 
and E.O. 14300, the agency is changing the period to file a motion in 
Sec.  2.323(e) from 10 days to 7 days; the period for responses is also 
reduced from 10 days to 7 days. This change is accompanied by a 
conforming change to Sec.  2.323(a)(2) clarifying that motions for 
reconsideration are not subject to the general 10-day timeline for 
motions. Further changes are also carried forward in Sec.  2.345(a)(1) 
to reflect a seven-day deadline for filing a petition for 
reconsideration and a seven-day answer period. Similarly, changes to 
Sec.  2.341(d) reduce the filing timeline for petitions for 
reconsideration before the Commission to seven days, with a seven-day 
answer period.

    The agency anticipates these changes will provide clarity for the 
parties and serve overall efficiency efforts. Also, seven-day filing 
periods should be sufficient because reconsideration is only warranted 
when the existing regulatory standard of compelling circumstances 
applies, such as in cases of a clear, material error that could not be 
reasonably anticipated.

Stays of Decisions and Application for a Stay

    Consistent with the streamlining efforts throughout 10 CFR part 2, 
the NRC is changing the Sec.  2.342(a) timeline for an application for 
a stay of the effectiveness of the decision or action pending filing of 
and a decision on a petition for review; the NRC is reducing the filing 
deadline from 10 days after service of a decision or action of a 
presiding officer to 7 days. This change is paired with a revision to 
Sec.  2.342(d) to clarify that the period for any party to file an 
answer supporting or opposing the granting of a stay is seven days 
after service of an application for a stay.
    Under existing Sec.  2.1213, any application for a stay of the 
effectiveness of the NRC staff's action on a matter involved in a 
hearing must be filed with the presiding officer within seven days of 
the issuance of the notice of the NRC staff's action under Sec.  
2.1202(a). While the agency is not altering this timeline, the agency 
is reducing the corresponding timeline in Sec.  2.1213(c) for any party 
or the NRC staff to file an answer supporting or opposing the granting 
of a stay from 10 days to 7 days after service of an application for a 
stay of the NRC staff's action.
    These modest timeline reductions should not significantly impact 
the burden on the parties to address the limited requirements and 
capped length of stay applications and associated answers. Further, 
these timeline changes are consistent with changes in this rule for 
similar filings while advancing the directives of the ADVANCE Act and 
E.O. 14300.
    Further, in response to a public comment on the proposed rule, the 
NRC is amending Sec.  2.1213(a) to clarify that the Commission will 
make decisions on applications to stay the effectiveness of an NRC 
staff order in a license transfer proceeding. Rulings on such

afforded if the Commission maintains its authority for deciding stay

Delivery of Hard Copy Documents

    Under existing Sec.  2.302, litigants must generally utilize the 
NRC's electronic filing system unless they (1) obtain an exemption from 
that requirement by demonstrating good cause to use a nonelectronic 
means of transmission for electronic documents on optical storage media 
or to file paper documents, or else (2) file without an exemption a 
document containing electronic portions that may not be transmitted via 
the E-Filing system for reasons of security or electronic format. In 
recent years these circumstances have been rare, and the NRC 
anticipates they will arise even less frequently going forward. When an 
alternative to electronic transmission is used, however, Sec.  2.306 
automatically extends the timeframes in 10 CFR part 2 to account for 
the additional time it will take for nonelectronic transmission of the 
document. Collectively, these extensions could considerably delay a 
proceeding. Therefore, the NRC is amending Sec.  2.306(b) to direct the 
presiding officer to establish whether, and how long, the timeframes in 
10 CFR part 2 should be extended in cases when nonelectronic 
transmission is allowed. Prior to this presiding officer order, the NRC 
is retaining the existing extensions of time in Sec.  2.306. In 
considering the need to extend the timeframes to account for 
nonelectronic service of documents, the presiding officer should ensure 
that the extensions will not cumulatively challenge timely completion 
of the adjudication.

    This analysis uses current contested hearing procedures for 
licensing proceedings under 10 CFR part 2 as the baseline and evaluates 
the changes in this rule as the regulatory alternative and estimates 
the final rule's costs and cost savings for the first five years of 
implementation of the rule.\21\ The final rule addresses many different 
types of applications, from applications to construct or operate 
reactors, to applications to construct or operate significant materials 
facilities, to applications for license renewals, amendments, and 
transfers, as well as applications associated with the proposed restart 
of reactors in decommissioning. Past experience suggests that, 
depending on the type of application, there is a greater or lesser 
probability that a hearing request will be filed or that a hearing 
request, if granted, will proceed to an evidentiary hearing. For 
example, previous 10 CFR part 52 early site permit and combined license 
applications for large reactors were nearly always the subject of a 
hearing request, while reactor license amendment applications are 
rarely challenged. Power reactor license renewal applications are often 
contested. Regarding the likelihood that an evidentiary hearing will be 
held, of the eight combined license applications for large reactors 
that were granted, an evidentiary hearing was held on four of these 
applications. There is a lower rate of holding evidentiary hearings for 
early site permit and reactor license renewal applications, but 
contested uranium recovery applications have led to a number of 
evidentiary hearings in the past 10 years. Past experience is to some 
degree informative, but any effort to extrapolate from this experience 
will be subject to substantial uncertainty. In addition, there is 
uncertainty in predicting how many applications of various types will 
be submitted or how many will be challenged.

Resource Projections for Next Five Years Based on the Final Rule

    The final rule makes a number of changes that affect the resources 
of litigants:

 For the initial filings (hearing requests/contentions, 
answers, and replies), the final rule accelerates the schedule for 
filings and decisions thereon, which could save a modest amount of 
resources. However, participants might compensate for this to some 
degree by concentrating their resources during the shorter filing and 
decision periods.

 The final rule saves substantial resources during the 
intermediate phase, between admission of contentions and the 
evidentiary hearing. Currently, evidentiary hearings are not held until 
the staff completes its review. This has led to lengthy intermediate 
periods where parties periodically update their document disclosures 
(and for the staff, the hearing file) and engage in other litigation 
activities. The NRC staff will no longer have to produce a hearing 
file, and the much shorter intermediate period would limit the 
disclosure burdens of the other parties, as well as limit burdens from 
other litigation activities during the intermediate period. Further, 
this final rule excludes some high-volume, low value internal 
electronic communications from disclosure, which should alleviate 
burdens on parties making document disclosures.

 The final rule will also save substantial resources during 
the evidentiary hearing phase. The existing model milestones in subpart 
L of 10 CFR part 2 envision an evidentiary hearing phase of about nine 
months from a triggering event to an initial decision, and in practice 
the evidentiary hearing phase has on average taken substantially longer 
than this. Under the final rule, the evidentiary hearing phase will 
generally be limited to between 2 to 4.5 months, with 3.5 to 4.5 months 
being the set period for most proceedings. Also, the schedule could 
only be extended if extraordinary circumstances necessitate a delay. A 
much shorter evidentiary hearing phase will inherently limit the number 
of filings and other litigation activities and otherwise limit the 
resources that can be expended. Nonetheless, these resource savings 
would only accrue if an evidentiary hearing is held.
    Considering these factors together, the NRC estimates that the NRC 
staff's resource burdens will drop from 4,150 hours to 3,025 hours per 
proceeding in which a hearing request is filed. Applicants are expected 
to see a drop in resource burden from 3,925 hours per contested 
proceeding to 3,025 hours. The NRC staff will see a larger resource 
savings than the applicant because of the elimination of the staff's 
hearing file obligations. Finally, the NRC estimates a modest drop in 
petitioner resource expenditures from 1,975 hours per contested 
proceeding to about 1,525 hours (about half of the applicant's resource 
expenditures).
    In this final rule, the NRC estimates a greater per-proceeding 
resources savings for litigants than it estimated in the proposed rule. 
This difference generally results from two changes from the proposed to 
final rule. First, in most licensing proceedings, the proposed rule 
would have required litigants to provide more information on the merits 
of proposed contentions in their initial filings, which would have 
increased resource burdens somewhat at the initial filing stage. 
Accelerating the resolution of contested issues by including more 
information on the merits in initial filings was intended to bring 
about a compensating burden reduction for those contentions that are 
admitted, but this reduction would have been limited to contentions 
that were admitted and proceeded to an evidentiary hearing (whereas 
most proposed contentions are not admitted and some admitted 
contentions are resolved before an evidentiary hearing is held). In 
total, the proposed rule provision was expected to increase resource 
burdens on participants to save some time in the overall schedule--this 
proposal has not been adopted in this final rule. Second, the proposed 
rule would have accelerated filings and decisions on standing to save 
some litigant resources associated with the filing of contentions in 
circumstances where standing is not demonstrated. Estimated resource 
savings here would have been limited because presiding officers usually 
find that petitioners demonstrate standing, and a substantial amount of 
litigant resources would have been expended on litigation of 
contentions by the time a decision on standing would have been issued. 
However, the proposal to accelerate the consideration of standing has 
been eliminated in this final rule for reasons discussed in this notice 
and in response to comments. Ultimately, eliminating both of these 
proposed rule provisions results in a modest resource savings for 
litigants in comparison to the proposed rule.
    For NRC adjudicatory decision-making staff, the NRC estimates that 
the resource burdens in proceedings where a hearing request is filed 
will drop from 4,700 hours per proceeding to 3,900 hours per 
proceeding. This estimated resource savings accounts for the following 
factors:

 Significantly reduced periods for presiding officer 
decision-making limit the resources that would be employed. For 
example, currently, there is about a 3.5-month period, on average, 
between submission of a contention and a ruling thereon. However, under 
the new final rule, this period is reduced to about 1.5 to 2.5 months. 
In addition, as stated above, evidentiary hearings take 9 months or 
longer under existing regulations, while most evidentiary hearings 
under the new final rule will take about 3.5 to 4.5 months total.

 However, savings from the reduced time periods will be 
limited by the following factors: (1) presiding officers might 
compensate for shorter periods to some degree by concentrating their 
resources during the shorter decision periods, (2) there will less 
likely be overlap in time spent by Licensing Board members on multiple 
proceedings in active litigation at the same time because the 
litigation period for each proceeding will be shorter, leading to less 
overlap in active litigation, and (3) evidentiary hearings are expected

resources savings for NRC adjudicatory decision-making staff than it 
estimated in the proposed rule. That is because the final rule does not 
include the proposed rule's provision on accelerating the consideration 
of standing, which was assumed to save some resources for adjudicatory 
decision-making staff on contentions in those cases where the presiding 
officer concluded that standing was not demonstrated, and because the 
final rule does not include milestones for Commission decisions on 
appeal, which was assumed to save resources through reduced periods for 
adjudicatory decision making.

factors, so the estimate of resource savings under the new requirements

    Over the five-year analysis period (2026-2030), the final rule 
revisions are projected to yield net savings for the public, the 
industry, and government. The combined net savings will generate 
cumulative undiscounted savings of $67.4 million (savings minus costs). 
Using 2025 as the base year, the net present value (NPV) of these net 
savings is $61.7 million, discounted at 3 percent, or $55.2 million, 
discounted at 7 percent. The projected annualized cost savings will be 
$13.5 million discounted at 3 percent, or $13.5 million discounted at 7 
percent.
    Because the final rule streamlines existing hearing procedures, the 
cost of implementing this rule for the hearing participants is expected 
to be minimal. The NRC does not currently have empirical data to 
quantify incremental implementation or transition-related effects 
associated with the accelerated filing schedules and the revised 
hearing provisions. Consistent with OMB Circular A-4, when impacts 
cannot be reliably monetized, agencies provide a qualitative 
assessment. Accordingly, the agency has examined potential 
implementation and transition effects and determined them to be minimal 
since the rule streamlines internal agency proceedings without 
significantly changing the basic adjudicatory framework.
    This final rule retains the existing approach to hearing requests 
by noticing opportunities for hearing after docketing and requiring a 
demonstration of standing and contention admissibility for a hearing 
request to be granted. The criteria for standing are unchanged, and the 
contention admissibility standards have been refined, without being 
raised. If a hearing request is granted, the agency still generally 
employs the same types of procedural mechanisms for evidentiary 
hearings as under the existing rules (e.g., written testimony and 
position statements, oral hearings, proposed findings of fact and 
conclusions of law), although the

presiding officer will have greater flexibility to determine which 
procedural mechanisms to use in a particular hearing. Adjudicatory 
schedules have been significantly changed, which will require greater 
discipline on the part of participants to meet those schedules, but 
participants will still face the same basic task of managing time and 
resources. The NRC also retains other procedural mechanisms, such as 
motions, summary disposition, standards for reopening the record, 
discovery, appeals, stay requests, and requests for reconsideration. 
Participants will have to familiarize themselves with changes to some 
of these procedural mechanisms (e.g., application of reopening

expected to be minimal.

XV. Severability

    This final rule makes changes to the requirements for contested 
hearings in NRC licensing proceedings. For the reasons described 
previously and in response to comments, the NRC has determined that its 
authority to promulgate these changes is well-supported in law and 
practice and should be upheld in any legal challenge. However, in the 
event that any portion of this rule is declared invalid, the NRC 
intends that the remaining portions be severable and continue in 
effect. Specifically, the NRC has independently considered each of 
those provisions in this rule, and intends that, if any of the 
provisions of this rule (or the application thereof to any person or 
circumstance) is held to be invalid by a court, such invalidity would 
not affect other provisions or application of such provisions to other 
persons or circumstances that can be given effect without the invalid 
provision or application. For example:

 This rule includes provisions for different types of 
applications. If the provisions for one type of application are held to 
be invalid, the provisions for other types of applications should 
continue in effect since these other provisions are not intertwined 
with the provisions held to be invalid and were independently 
considered, with their own supporting basis and analysis.

 This rule provides scheduling provisions for several 
procedural categories, including hearing requests, intervention 
petitions, contentions, motions, discovery, petitions for review, 
interlocutory appeals, requests for interlocutory review, stay 
requests, requests for reconsideration, and evidentiary hearings. If 
the schedule requirements for one procedural category are held to be 
invalid, the schedule requirements for other procedural categories 
should remain in effect because the schedules for each procedural 
category are not intertwined and were independently considered, with 
their own supporting basis and analysis.

 In addition to schedule provisions, the rule includes 
changes to various procedural categories, including changes to 
definitions, Federal Register notices, contention standards, the 
reopening standards, discovery requirements, selection of hearing 
procedures, actions the staff can take during the pendency of a 
hearing, evidentiary hearings, additional procedures in Sec.  2.1214 
for license transfer proceedings, procedures for referred rulings and 
certified questions, and provisions for computation of time associated 
with delivery of hard copy documents. If the provisions for one type of 
procedural category are held to be invalid, the provisions for other 
types of procedural categories should continue in effect since these 
other provisions are not intertwined with the provisions held to be 
invalid and were independently considered, with their own supporting 
basis and analysis.
    In addition, to the extent there are multiple changes in a 
category, if one of the changes in the category is held to be invalid, 
the other changes in the category should continue in effect because 
these changes were independently considered, with their own supporting 
basis and analysis. Examples include the various definitional changes; 
the two refinements to the contention admissibility criteria; the 
different reopening changes (e.g., the Sec.  2.326(a) change, the 
provisions in each sentence of Sec.  2.326(e)(1), and the change in 
Sec.  2.326(e)(2)); the various discovery changes (e.g., elimination of 
subpart L hearing file, limitation on NRC staff's Sec.  2.336 
disclosures, exclusion of draft documents from Sec.  2.336 disclosures, 
exclusion of certain internal communications from Sec.  2.336 
disclosures, changes to discovery schedules); the evidentiary hearing 
procedure changes; and the changes in each paragraph of Sec.  2.1214.
    Finally, for all of the matters described in the previous 
paragraphs, the agency's purpose in making its proceedings timely and 
efficient would best be effectuated by applying the provisions in this 
final rule to the maximum practicable extent.
